ORDER: (Per the Honíble The Acting Chief Justice Ramesh Ranganathan)
The proceedings under challenge in this writ petition is the
assessment order dated 28.12.2002 and the revised assessment
proceedings dated 29.12.2006.
The only ground, on which the assessment order, passed five years
before the writ petition, was filed is questioned is that a copy of the
assessment order was not served on the petitioner; and the conditions
stipulated in Rule 58 of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Rules,
1957 (for short ìthe APGST Rulesî) have not been complied with. The
petitioner has, admittedly, closed his business in August, 2000 itself.
Rule 53(a) of the APGST Rules stipulates that, if any dealer discontinues
the whole or any part of the business carried on by him, he shall inform
the fact to the assessing authority concerned within 30 days thereafter.
The petitioner has, admittedly, not intimated the respondent-assessing
authority of the fact that they had discontinued their business, nor did
they intimate the assessing authority of the address to which notices or
summons should be sent. In the counter affidavit, the respondent states
that the notice was served by affixture on the premises where the
petitioner had hitherto carried on business as a dealer.
While Sri S.Krishna Murthy, learned counsel for the petitioner,
would contend that Rule 58 of the APGST Rules has not been complied
with, it is necessary to note that Rule 58(d) of the APGST Rules stipulates
that, if any or all of the modes i.e (a) to (c) is not practicable, then the
notice can be served by affixture on some conspicuous place at his last
known place of business or residence. Clause (a) of Rule 58 could not
have been complied with as the petitioner has, admittedly, not informed
the respondent-assessing authority of his address to enable them to

at his last known place of business or residence and, as the business
premises was closed, the respondent cannot be faulted in this regard.
Clause (c) requires notice to be sent by registered post and, if it is
returned unserved, for it to be put on the notice board of the office of the
assessing authority or in the Chamber of Commerce. No useful purpose

ORDER : The Court Made the following order :-
The petitioners who are arrayed as accused nos.1 to 3,
apprehend arrest at the hands of the respondent police for an
alleged offence punishable under Sections 417,420 and 506(i) of IPC
in Crime No.194 of 2016, seek anticipatory bail.

2. The case of the prosecution is that the defacto complainant
is the owner of the property in R.S.No.171/4 in Kallivelipatti
Village of Vadipatti Taluk, Madurai District. The first petitioner
sold the property as the power agent to second petitioner and on
complaint, a case has been registered against the petitioners.

3. The learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the
first petitioner is the power agent of defacto complainant. He has
been appointed by the deed of Power dated 03.05.1995 bearing
Doc.No.34 of 1995. The first petitioner sold the property as a
power agent of the defacto complainant, to the second petitioner
herein on 09.10.2003 bearing Doc.No.1564 of 2003. The second
petitioner received summons from the Land Grabbing Special Cell for
enquiry on 01.03.2013 and she has also appeared. At the time of
enquiry, she came to know that the defacto complainant executed
another power of attorney on 13.04.2009 bearing Doc.No.78 of 2009,
appointing one O.Raja as her power agent and he sold the property
to one Shanmugapriyan. Thereafter, the said Shanmugapriyan sold to
one Muthusamy by registered sale deed dated 21.02.2013, bearing
Doc. No.752 of 2013. Therefore, the second petitioner lodged a
complaint before the respondent Police and the respondent police
did not receive the same. Therefore, the second petitioner filed
Crl.O.P.(MD).No.6110 of 2016 for a direction to register thehttps://hcservices.ecourts.gov.in/hcservices/
2
complaint and this Court Court by order dated 22.04.2016, directed
the respondent police to conduct enquiry and register the case.
Thereafter, the defacto complainant gave a present complaint on
28.04.2016 by suppressing the earlier enquiry conducted by the
Inspector of Police Land Grabbing Cell. He further submitted that
the petitioners are innocent and they have not committed any
offence as alleged by the prosecution and their names have been
falsely implicated in this case.

4. The learned Government Advocate (Crl. Side) submitted that
this is the civil dispute and the investigation of the case is
pending.

5. Considering the fact that the first petitioner was
appointed by the defacto complainant as her power agent and he has
sold the property as the power agent in the year 1995 to the second
petitioner and the same has been registered in Doc.No.1564 of
2003, dated 09.10.2003 and after attending enquiry conducted by the
Inspector of Land Grabbing Special Cell, the second petitioner
lodged a complaint on 04.03.2016 and filed Crl.O.P(MD).No.6110 of
2016 before this Court and this Court directed the respondent
Police to register a complaint and in such circumstances,
suppressing the earlier facts the defacto complainant has given a
complaint against the petitioners and hence this Court inclined to
grant anticipatory bail to the petitioners. Accordingly, the
petitioners are ordered to be released on bail in the event of
arrest or on their appearance, within a period of fifteen days from
the date of receipt of a copy of this order, before the learned
Judicial Magistrate, Vadipatti, Madurai District on condition that
each of the petitioners shall execute a bond for a sum of
Rs.10,000/- (Rupees ten thousand only) with two sureties each for a
like sum to the satisfaction of the respondent police or the
police officer who intends to arrest or to the satisfaction of the
learned Magistrate concerned and on further condition that:
[a] the petitioners shall report before the respondent
police daily at 10.00 am for a period of two weeks and thereafter,
as and when required for interrogation.
[b] the petitioners shall not tamper with evidence or witness
either during investigation or trial.
[c] the petitioners shall not abscond either during
investigation or trial.
[d] On breach of any of the aforesaid conditions, the learned
Magistrate/Trial Court is entitled to take appropriate action
against the petitioners in accordance with law as if the conditions
have been imposed and the petitioners released on bail by the
learned Magistrate/Trial Court himself as laid down by the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in P.K.Shaji vs. State of Kerala [(2005)AIR SCW
5560].
6.The Inspector of Police concerned is directed to send a
compliance report to the office of the learned Government Advocate,https://hcservices.ecourts.gov.in/hcservices/

not.

ORDER
The short grievance of the petitioner, a House
Building Society is against the arguable long pendency of
its case in CO.APP.NO.245/2019 pending before the Karnataka
Appellate Tribunal, Bangalore.
2. The official respondents are represented by learned
AGA; notice to respondent Nos. 3 to 22 is dispensed with since
they are neither necessary nor proper parties and also because
they will have audience before the Tribunal when the appeal is
taken up for consideration.
3. The Apex Court in a catena of decisions has held
that right to speedy justice is part of Articles 14 & 21 of the
Constitution of India and therefore judicial & quasi judicial
6
functionaries have to keep this in mind while treating the cause
brought before them.
In view of the above, this writ petition is disposed off
directing the Karnataka Appellate Tribunal to consider &
dispose off the appeal in question within a period of six months,
all contentions having been kept open.
All the respondents including those to whom no notice is
issued and all stakeholders shall be heard in the subject

The above appeal is filed by the accused in
Sessions Case No. 340 of 2004 on the file of the
Additional Sessions Judge, Fast Track Court-1,
Palakkad.

2. The Sub Inspector of Police, Malampuzha charge
sheeted the accused alleging offence under Section
55(a) of the Abkari Act.

3. The prosecution case is that on 3.11.2002 at 5
p.m., the accused was found in possession of 15
bottles (15 x 180ml) of Indian Made Foreign Liquor in
an unnumbered shed in Manakkalkadu in Malampuzha II
Village.

4. To substantiate the case, the prosecution
examined PW1 to PW4. Exhibits P1 to P7 are the
documents marked on the side of the prosecution. MO1
series are the material objects marked in this case.

5. After going through the evidence and
CRL.APPEAL No.1117 OF 2005 3
documents, the trial court found that, the accused
committed the offence under Section 55(a) of the
Abkari Act. He is sentenced to undergo Simple
imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a
fine of Rs.1,00,000/-. In default of payment of fine,
the accused is directed to undergo Simple imprisonment
for a further period of three months. Aggrieved by the
conviction and sentence, this Crl.Appeal is filed.

6. Heard the learned counsel for the appellant
and the learned Public Prosecutor.

7. The learned Counsel for the appellant
submitted that, the investigation in this case is
conducted by PW4, the Sub Inspector of Police,
Hemambika Nagar Police Station. He is not an
authorized person as per the Abkari Act to conduct
investigation in this case because the alleged search
and seizure in this case was within the jurisdiction
of Malampuzha Police Station. The learned Counsel also
submitted that, even though the seizure of the alleged
contraband article was on 3.11.2002, the same was
produced before the court only on 8.11.2002.
CRL.APPEAL No.1117 OF 2005 4

8. The learned Public Prosecutor submitted that,
in the light of the oral and documentary evidence, in
this case, the prosecution proved the case. He argued
that the trial court convicted the accused based on
the legal evidence adduced by the prosecution. The
learned Public Prosecutor submitted that there is
nothing to interfere with the conviction and sentence
imposed by the trial court.

9. The point for consideration in this appeal is
whether the accused committed the offence under
Section 55(a) of the Abkari Act.

10. Admittedly, the search and seizure, in this
case, was from a place within the jurisdiction of
Malampuzha Police Station. PW4 is the Sub Inspector of
Police of Hemambika Police Station. There is no
evidence before this court to show that there is any
notification authorizing PW4 to investigate this case.
The learned Public Prosecutor produced an order
No.1968/DR/E/02 dated 3.11.2002 of the Circle
Inspector of Police, Town North, Palakkkad by which
the Sub Inspector of Police, Hemambika Nagar Police
CRL.APPEAL No.1117 OF 2005 5
Station is authorized to investigate Crime No.101 of
2002. Admittedly, this order is not produced before
the trial court, and therefore, I am not in a position
to accept the same. Moreover, even if this order is
there, it is a settled position that, a Circle
Inspector of Police has no jurisdiction to authorize
a Sub Inspector to conduct investigation in an Abkari
case outside the jurisdiction of his Police station.
In this case, admittedly, PW4 is the Sub Inspector of
Hemambika Nagar Police Station and he has no
territorial jurisdiction over the Malampuzha Police
Station. Therefore, he has no jurisdiction to
investigate the case registered by the Malampuzha
Police Station. This point is considered by this Court
in Narayanankutty v. State of Kerala [2015(1) KHC
702]. The relevant paragraphs of the above decision
are extracted hereunder:
“7. PW6 deposed that he had taken over the
investigation in this case as directed by the
Circle Inspector of Police, Hemambika Nagar, on
12.07.2003. A Circle Inspector of Police is
competent under SRO No.321 of 1996 to conduct
investigation of a case within his territorial
CRL.APPEAL No.1117 OF 2005 6
jurisdiction. He cannot delegate such power
given to him under SRO No.321 of 1996 to a
subordinate Police Officer because, such a
power can be conferred only by a notification
issued by the Government under Section 4 of the
Abkari Act. The direction issued by the Circle
Inspector of Police to PW6 for conducting
investigation cannot be equated with a
notification issued under Section 4 of the
Abkari Act. Therefore, the authority granted by
the Circle Inspector of Police cannot be a
ground for exercising jurisdiction by a Sub
Inspector of Police beyond his territorial
jurisdiction.
8. As the investigation was conducted by
PW6, an incompetent officer, the court below
had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the
offence alleged in the complaint filed based on
such investigation. Consequently, the court
be

11. Moreover, the seizure of the contraband
property from the accused was on 3.11.2002. The
property was produced before court only on 8.11.2002.
When PW4 was cross-examined regarding the delay in
producing the property before the court, he deposed
that, there is no reason for the delay. This point is
also considered by this Court in Sukumaran v. State
of Kerala (2019(3) KLT 920), Ravi v. State-Sub
Inspector of Police, Meppadi (2018(5) KHC 352) and
Vikraman v. State of Kerala (2018(1) KLT 822).
Relevant portion of the judgment in Ravi's case
(supra) is extracted hereunder:
“8. In order to support the argument, the
learned counsel for the appellant cited the
ruling in Ramankutty v. Excise Inspector,
Chelannur Range, 2013(3) KHC 308 : 2013(3) KLJ
434 : ILR 2013 (3) Ker. 535 : 2013(3) KLT SN 83
wherein it is held that 'in the absence of
satisfactory explanation by the prosecution
CRL.APPEAL No.1117 OF 2005 8
showing the cause of delay, even delay of one
day is fatal to the prosecution and therefore,
the accused is entitled to the benefit of
doubt.
9. In the instant case, there is a delay of
four days in producing the contraband articles
before the court. According to the evidence of
PW4, it was kept under his safe custody. But,
he has to explain that these contraband
articles were produced before the court with
tamper proof. Moreover, Ext.P6 is the copy of
the forwarding note. It does not contain the
seal, which was alleged to have affixed on the
sample. So, without verifying the sample seal,
the court cannot act upon Ext.P6 copy of the
forwarding note."
Since, in this case, there is no explanation for not
producing the contraband article before the court
immediately after seizure, the accused is entitled the
benefit of doubt on this ground also.

12. In the light of the above discussions, I think
the accused is entitled the benefit of doubt.
Hence, this Criminal Appeal is allowed. The
conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant as
per the judgment dated 8.6.2005 in S.C No.340 of 2004
CRL.APPEAL No.1117 OF 2005 9
on the file of the Additional Sessions Judge, Fast
Track Court-1, Palakkad, is set aside. The appellant
is set at liberty. Bail bond, if any, executed by the
appellant, is cancelled.

3. "Every day's delay must be
explained" does not mean that a
pedantic approach should be made.
Why not every hour's delay, every
second's delay? The doctrine must
be applied in a rational common
sense pragmatic manner.
4. When substantial justice and
technical considerations are pitted
against each other, cause of
substantial justice deserves to be
preferred for the other side cannot
claim to have vested right in
injustice being done because of a
non-deliberate delay.

5. There is no presumption that
delay is occasioned deliberately,
or on account of culpable
negligence, or on account of mala
fides. A litigant does not stand to
benefit by resorting to delay. In
fact he runs a serious risk.

6. It must be grasped that
judiciary is respected not on
account of its power to legalize
injustice on technical grounds but
because it is capable of removing
injustice and is expected to do
so.”
5. Having heard the learned advocate for the
applicant and considering the averments made
Page 3 of 4
C/CA/658/2023 ORDER DATED: 21/07/2023
in the application and as the delay is
sufficiently explained and in view of the
facts and circumstances of the case, the
delay of 103 days occurred in filing the
appeal deserves to be condoned and is hereby
condoned.
6. Accordingly, the present application is
allowed.
(GITA GOPI,J)

12. Learned counsels for the respondents have

13. On the other hand, learned counsel for claimants

Registration number of offending vehicle and

under Section 133 of Motor Vehicles Act was served

and there is no protest on the part of respondents qua

Therefore, it is sufficient to conclude rash and negligent

for the claimants further contended that mere non-

Though no eye-witness has been examined by claimants,

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
14. On consideration of respective arguments raised
by both the parties, I am in agreement with the
arguments advanced by learned counsel for the
petitioners that mere non-examination of eye-witness by
itself is no ground to doubt the involvement of
respondent / driver and offending vehicle in the
accident. The involvement of driver and offending
vehicle is dependent upon the facts and circumstances of
each case. Motor Vehicles Act is beneficial legislature
enacted to provide relief to accident victims without
being bogged down by technicalities of law of evidence
and also keeping in view socio-economic conditions
prevalent in society.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
15. In
Gurdeep Kaur Vs. Tarsem Singh, 2008 (2)
RCR (Civil) 774, it was held that the Tribunals
established under the Motor Vehicles Act, are not
governed by the rules of procedure envisaged by the
Civil Procedure Code and the Tribunals are required to
evolve their own procedure to meet the ends of justice,
based on the principles of natural justice, equity and
good conscience. The proceedings before the Tribunal
are of summary nature wherein inquiry has to be
conducted and the evidence is not to be scrutinized, in
the manner, as is done in a civil or in a criminal case. In
a criminal case, the rule is of proof beyond reasonable
doubt and in civil cases, the rule is preponderance of
probabilities and if there is some evidence before the
Claims Tribunal to prove a fact, no nicety, doubt or
suspicion should weigh with it, in deciding a Motor
Accident Claims case. Hon’ble Delhi High Court in
National Insurance Company Limited Vs. Pushpa
Rana & Ors., 2009 ACJ 287 (Delhi High Court) had
held that certified copy of criminal court, such as, FIR,
recovery memo and mechanical inspection report of
vehicle are the documents of sufficient proof to reach the
conclusion that driver was negligent and proceedings
under Motor Vehicles Act are not akin to proceedings in
a civil suit and hence, strict rules of evidence are not
required to be followed in a claim case before Tribunal.
In
Lakhu Singh Vs. Uday Singh, 2008 (1) RCR (Civil)
VIRENDRA SINGH ADHIKARI
2026.01.31 19:00
I attest to the accuracy and
integrity of this document
FAO-2148-2025 (O&M) -7-
805 (P&H), it was held that while considering a claim
petition, the Tribunal is required to hold an inquiry and
not to act as a Criminal Court so as to find whether the
claimants have established the occurrence beyond any
shadow of doubt. In the inquiry, if there is prima facie
evidence of the occurrence, there is no reason to
disbelieve such evidence. The statements of witnesses
coupled with the facts of registration of FIR and trial of
the accused in a criminal court are sufficient to arrive at
conclusion that the accident has taken place. Therefore,
case of claimants has to be tested upon touchstone of
standard of proof i.e. ‘preponderance of probabilities’.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
16. Admittedly no eye witness was examined by the
claimants. PW-3 has fairly admitted that he had not
witnessed the accident. The case of claimants is,
therefore, dependent upon the circumstances, from
which the involvement of offending vehicle and rash and
negligent driving on the part of its driver has to be
gathered. On the other hand case is being opposed by
respondents for non examination of eye-witness by the
claimants and as respondent No. 1 while appearing as
RW-1 has denied the accident in totality.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
17. Eye witness account of accident is the easiest
method to prove accident and negligence of driver of
offending vehicle. However, it is not the only way to
determine issue of negligence. Accident is sudden
occurrence and many a times eye witness is not
available or even if available is either won over by other
side or is not interested in deposing in the Court for
various reasons. The reasons are many for such attitude.
As per law, a fact can be established by way of direct
evidence or by circumstantial evidence. Maxim ‘
res ipsa
loquitur’ i.e. “t
he thing speaks for itself” is also
applicable to motor accident claim cases. Therefore,
even in absence of direct eye witness account, Court can
find out whether accident had taken place on account of
negligent driving of driver of offending vehicle from the
circumstantial evidence available on record on the
touchstone of standard of proof “preponderance of
probability”.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
18. To prove their case, claimants have relied upon
the contents of FIR No. 537 dated 26.11.2022, seizure
memo dated 26.11.2022 vide which offending vehicle
and bicycle of deceased were taken into police
possession from the spot, notice under Section 133 of
Motor Vehicles Act dated 28.11.2022 and mechanical

examination report of offending vehicle dated

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
19. In the present case, perusal of FIR and complaint
made by PW-3 to police, both forming part of Ex. P-4,
shows that manner of accident and registration number
of offending Bus are mentioned with consistent details
by author of FIR i.e. PW-3. The contents of FIR have
been duly proved by PW-3 being author of FIR.
Claimants in their claim petition as well as claimant No.
3 / author of FIR while appearing as PW3 had described
the manner of accident as pleaded by claimants and as
was stated by him while lodging the FIR. Within few
hours of the accident, the registration number and make
of offending vehicle had come in public domain. Perusal
of seizure memo dated 26.11.2022 (forming part of Ex.
P-4) goes to show that ill-fated bicycle and offending
Bus were taken into police possession from the spot itself
on 26.11.2022. Registration number of offending vehicle
was mentioned in FIR, accordingly, Investigating Officer
served notice dated 28.11.2022 under Section 133 of the
MV Act (forming part of final report under Section 173
Cr.P.C. Ex. P-4) upon respondent No. 2. Proprietor of
respondent No. 2 namely Sanjeev Kumar son of Shri
Jogi Ram had made his written endorsement on the said
notice itself that his firm is owner of offending Bus and
on 26.11.2022, Naveen son of Shri Ram Karan, resident
of village Mehlana, District Sonipat i.e. respondent No.
1 was driving their Bus and he assured to produce
respondent No. 1 before police at the earliest. In
response to the said notice, respondent No. 2 had not
denied that his Bus never met with an accident and he
simply disclosed that respondent No. 1 was the driver on
his Bus on 26.11.2022 and he instead of denying
involvement of their vehicle in the accident had stated
that he would produce respondent No. 1 as soon as
possible. The mechanical examination of offending Bus,
which was taken in possession on 26.11.2022 from spot,
was conducted on 28.11.2022 i.e. within two days of the
accident. Vide report dated 28.11.2022 annexed with
report under Section 173 Cr.P.C. Ex. P-4, as per which
following damages were found by the Motor Mechanic :-
➢ Bend below the left front bumper and head light
with broken left indicator;

2026.01.31 19:00

FAO-2148-2025 (O&M) -9-
➢ Dent under the rear brake light and removed
paint; and
➢ Scratches on the right side and paint removed;
Respondents No. 1 and 2 have failed to explain presence
of their vehicle at the sp

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
20. In view of the above mentioned circumstances,
which corroborate the contents of FIR and testimony of
PW-3, mere nonexamination of eye witness in the
present case is not fatal to the case of claimants. The
findings upon the issue of negligence are totally
dependent upon the facts and circumstances of each
case. There is no hard and fast rule that in each and
every case negligence can only be proved by examining
eye-witness. It is also not mandatory to believe eye-
witness account if an eye-witness is examined. It all is
dependent upon the facts and appreciation of evidence
in each case. The Court has to conclude rashness and
negligence as per the facts and circumstances placed
before it by way of admissible evidence. Respondent No.
1 while appearing as RW-1 has asserted that though, he
was on duty on the offending vehicle on 26.11.2022, but
his Bus had not met with any accident and asserted his
false implication. However, in his cross-examination,
RW-1 has admitted that he has not made any complaint
regarding his alleged false implication, registration of
FIR against him and framing of charges against him.
Besides his self-serving testimony, which also does not
inspire confidence, no evidence has been led by
respondent No. 1 to prove his assertions that no accident
was caused by him while driving offending Bus. RW-1
has failed to explain abandonment of offending vehicle
at place of accident and damage to it. Accordingly, the
self serving and uncorroborated assertions of
respondent No. 1 regarding total denial of accident and
involvement of offending vehicle and respondent No. 1 in
the accident are not believable, whereas the assertions
made by PW-3 and claimants are duly corroborated by
contents of FIR, recovery of offending vehicle from the
spot itself in damaged condition as well as conclusion of
investigating agency that accident had taken place due
VIRENDRA SINGH ADHIKARI
2026.01.31 19:00
I attest to the accuracy and
integrity of this document
FAO-2148-2025 (O&M) -10-
to rash and negligent driving on the part of respondent
No. 1. As such, the evidence led by claimants to prove
their case is more convincing than the bald statement of
respondent No. 1.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
21. Hon'ble High Court in
Girdhari Lal Vs. Radhey
Shyam, 1993 (2) PLR 109 had held that if the driver of
the offending vehicle is challaned by the police and is
facing trial for causing accident due to rash and
negligent driving, it is safe to presume that accident had
taken place due to rash and negligent driving on his
part. In present case after registration of FIR, matter
was investigated and as per investigation, investigating
agency had concluded that it was rash and negligent
driving on the part of respondent No. 1 while driving the
offending Bus, which resulted into accident leading to
loss of life of deceased Satyadev. This conclusion of
investigating agency was followed by filing of final
report under Section 173 Cr.P.C. (Ex. P-4) against
respondent No. 1 for the commission of offence
punishable under Section 279 / 304-A IPC and framing
of charges vide charge-sheet dated 15.02.2023, which is
part of Ex. P-4. Registration of FIR and trial of the
accused in a criminal Court are sufficient to arrive at
conclusion that the accident has taken place due to rash
and negligent driving of respondent No. 1 while driving
vehicle No. HR-69D-2499.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
22. There is also no evidence on record that
respondents No. 1 and 2 ever filed any representation
before higher authorities against alleged false
implication of respondent No. 1 and offending vehicle.
Their silence for such a long period also goes against
them.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
23. If the above mentioned circumstances, evidence
led by claimants, recovery of offending vehicle and ill-
fated bicycle from the spot, mechanical report dated
28.11.2022 showing damage to front portion of Bus, fact
that respondents have failed to rebut the case of
claimants and that it is respondent No. 1 who is facing
trial for causing accident without any protest, are tested
upon standard of proof i.e. preponderance of probability,
the only conclusion which can be drawn is that accident
in question resulting in the death of Satyadev took place
on account of rash and negligent driving on the part of
respondent No. 1 while driving the offending Bus
bearing registration No. HR-69D-2499. Issue No. 1 is
VIRENDRA SINGH ADHIKARI
2026.01.31 19:00

accordingly, decided in favour of claimants and against
respondents.
ISSUE NO. 2 :
Income of deceased & dependency of claimants :

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
24. Claimant No. 1 - wife and claimants No. 2 to 4 -
sons of deceased have sought compensation of Rs. 1.00
crore and asserted that deceased Satyadev was 46 years
old, employed with Den Block Private Limited Company,
Bahalgarh, District Sonipat and was drawing salary of
Rs. 17,000/- per month. These assertions have been
reiterated by his son namely Anurag while appearing in
the witness box as PW-3.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
25. To prove the employment and income of deceased
Satyadev, claimants have placed reliance upon the
testimony of PW-1 Sunil Kumar, Executive, M/s Den
Block Brakes, Bahalgarh, Sonipat. PW-1 had brought
the summoned record pertaining to employment and
salary of deceased with the said company and stated
that deceased Satyadev was working as Operator in
their company since 01.05.2012 and was drawing salary
of Rs. 13,396/- per month, which does not include the
incentive and overtime. He further asserted that
incentive for full attendance is Rs. 2,000/- and overtime
is paid separately. He tendered salary slips of deceased
as Ex. P-1 and Ex. P-2 as well as his authority letter as
Ex. P-3.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
26. In his cross-examination, PW-1 stated that as per
Ex. P-1 and Ex. P-2, deceased was the permanent
employee of their company.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
27. Perusal of salary slips Ex. P-1 for October, 2022
and Ex. P-2 for November, 2022 shows that deceased
was employed as Operator with the said company vide
employee ID No. 4010192 having ESI No. 1320077468
and mode of payment of salary was bank account No.
01911050098926 with HDFC Bank Ltd. Perusal of
salary slips Ex. P-1 and Ex. P-2 goes to show that gross
salary of deceased was Rs. 13,396/- per month. The
above mentioned evidence qua occupation and income
of deceased has gone unrebutted and no evidence to
prove to the contrary has been led by respondents. As
such, the evidence led by claimants with regard to
employment of deceased with said company and his
salary of Rs. 13,396/- per month is trustworthy.
Accordingly, the monthly income of deceased is taken as
Rs. 13,396/- per month.
VIRENDRA SINGH ADHIKARI
2026.01.31 19:00

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
28. Petitioners have pleaded age of deceased to be 46
years. In salary slips Ex. P-1 and Ex. P-2, date of birth
of deceased Satyadev is mentioned as 29.08.1976.
Accident had taken place on 26.11.2022. No evidence
has been led by either of the parties to prove the age of
the deceased to the contrary. Accordingly, the age of the
deceased is taken to be 46 years. Deceased was 46 years
of age and as such, multiplier of 13 has to be applied in
view of law laid down in
Smt. Sarla Verma & Ors. Vs.
Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr., 2009 (3) RCR
(Civil) 77. To determine loss of dependency, personal /
living expenses being incurred by deceased on himself
needs to be deducted from assessed notional monthly /
annual income of deceased. Keeping in view number of
dependents i.e. claimants, who are four, 1/4th of total
income needs to be deducted, towards personnel
expenses.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
29. Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in
National
Insurance Company Vs. Pranay Sethi and Ors., 2017
(4) RCR (Civil) 1009 has held that in case deceased was
self employed and earning established income and his /
her age was between 40 to 50 years, 25% amount has to
be added to the income towards future prospects.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
30. In view of law laid down in
National Insurance
Company Limited Vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors. (supra)
the claimants shall also be entitled to compensation of
Rs. 16,500/- as compensation for funeral expenses and
Rs. 16,500/- as compensation for loss of estate and
claimant No. 1 shall also be entitled to compensation of
Rs. 40,000/- for loss of spousal consortium.

labelled.court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
labelled.text:
31. Keeping in view age of deceased, after applying
future prospects to the extent of 25%, applying
multiplier of 13 and by deducting

Heard Mr. Devnani, learned AGP for the
petitioner – State and Mr. Patel, learned

2. The captioned petitions have arisen from
common award dated 30.11.2013 passed by learned
Labour Court at Himatnagar in Reference (LCH)
Nos. 151 of 2005, 152 of 2005, 153 of 2005, 155
of 2005, 32 of 2006, 33 of 2006, 34 of 2006, 35
of 2006, 41 of 2006 and 20 of 2009.
2.1 Both sides concerned in said reference cases
i.e. the workmen as well as the employer (i.e.
Dy. Executive Engineer) have taken out petitions
which are directed against the said common award.
Special Civil Application Nos.4042 of 2016, 4051
of 2016, 4043 of 2016 to 4049 of 2016 are filed
by the State whereas Special Civil Application
Nos.4215 of 2016 to 4221 of 2016 are filed by the
concerned workmen. Thus, the group of petitions
are cross petitions filed by both sides who felt
Page 2
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
aggrieved by common award.
2.2 Since common issues of law and similar facts
are involved in all petitions and since both
sides have made common submissions, the petitions
are decided by this common order.

3. With the allegation that the employer (Dy.
Executive Engineer), Irrigation Sub Division,
Meshwo Jalagar Project, illegally terminated
their service, 10 workmen raised industrial
dispute which came to be referred for
adjudication to learned Labour Court at
Himatnagar vide order of reference passed by
appropriate government. The learned Labour Court
registered the said reference as Reference (LCH)
Nos. 151 of 2005, 152 of 2005, 153 of 2005, 155
of 2005, 32 of 2006, 33 of 2006, 34 of 2006, 35
of 2006, 41 of 2006 and 20 of 2009.
3.1 In their statement of claim, the claimants
made almost similar allegations. The claimants
Page 3
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
alleged that they were working with the employer
State since more than 15 years and that they had
worked regularly and continuously, however,
despite such long service rendered by them, the
employer illegally terminated their service in
October 2003 by oral order and without following
procedure prescribed by law. With such
allegations, the claimants demanded that the
employer should reinstate them with consequential
benefits.
3.2 The opponent employer filed reply. In the
written statement, the opponent denied the
allegations. It was contended by the opponent
before the learned Labour Court that it is not
true that from the year 1986 to 30.10.2003,
respondent – workmen were working as labourer.
The employee claimed that the allegations should
not be believed because the workmen have not
produced any relevant documents to support this
contention. It was also stated that the
respondent – workmen were working as daily wager
Page 4
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
and were relieved on 30.10.2003 pursuant to
Government Resolution. Therefore, there is no
question arose about malpractice. It is also
stated that appointment of workmen was not as per
the recruitment rules and post is not sanctioned
and is not available on the establishment of the
Department. In case of irregular and illegal
appointments, there is no question of breach of
Industrial Disputes Act. It is also stated by the
employer that the work is completed. The workmen
were called for work, as and when the work was
available and on completion of work, the
department stopped calling/engaging the
claimants.
3.3 Upon conclusion of the proceedings, learned
Labour Court heard rival submissions. The learned
Labour Court thereafter, passed impugned common
award whereby learned Labour Court directed the
employer to reinstate 9 out of 10 claimants with
continuity of service b

4. So far as direction (award) passed in
Reference (LCH) No.41 of 2006 is concerned,
neither the heirs of original claimant nor the
employer have taken out any proceedings against
the direction to pay Rs.25,000/- in lieu of
reinstatement. Learned AGP declared that the said
sum of Rs.25,000/- is paid to the heirs of
original claimant which they have accepted.
4.1 Thus, in respect of one reference out of
total reference cases, there is no dispute and
present proceedings are confined to common award
in respect of 9 reference cases. The said 9
claimants are directed to be reinstated with
continuity of service.
Page 6
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
4.2 So far as petitions filed by the claimants
are concerned, it is necessary to note that the
claimants have taken out the petitions for
direction against the employer to implement the
award. Differently put, the original claimants
have not challenged the decision of learned
Labour Court denying backwages. The original
claimants have taken out the petitions to seek
arrears of salary from the date of award i.e.
30.11.2013 and for direction to the employer to
reinstate them. Differently put, the petitions
filed by the claimants are in nature of execution
petitions.

5. Therefore, actually, the issue on hand is the
challenge raised by the State against the
impugned award.
5.1 On plain reading of the award, it comes out
that the learned Labour Court has, upon
appreciation of evidence, believed and accepted
that:-
Page 7
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
[a] the claimants worked with the employer
for more than 15 years;
[b] the claimants worked regularly and
continuously for almost 15 years with the
employer;
[c] the employer terminated their service in
October 2003 without following prescribed
procedure and in violation of Section 25F of
I.D.Act;
[d] since the employer failed to place on
record original muster roll for entire period
of claimants' employment and since the
employer placed on record original muster
roll only for part of the total period during
which the claimants rendered service, it was
just and proper to draw adverse inference;
[e] by way of adverse inference, learned
Labour Court held that the claimants had
worked for more than 240 days and that
therefore, the employer could not have
terminated service of the claimants without
complying the conditions prescribed by
Page 8
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
Section 25F and that since said requirement
was not complied, the termination of service
of all claimants was illegal;
[f] Having reached such conclusion, learned
Labour Court addressed the issue about
appropriate relief; and
[g] After taking into account the evidence
available on record, learned Labour Court
considered it appropriate to decline the
demand for backwages, however, learned Labour
Court considered it appropriate to direct the
employer to reinstate the claimants on their
original post with continuity of service.

6. So far as above mentioned findings and
conclusion by learned Labour Court are concerned,
it is necessary and relevant to note that
according to the respondents, the claimants were
engaged irregularly and on ad hoc and daily wage
basis.
6.1 It is pertinent to note that the learned
Page 9
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
Labour Court has not recorded any conclusion
contrary to said assertion of employer.
6.2 On this count, it is also relevant to note
that:-
[i] the claimants did not place on record
appointment order;
[ii] the claimants did not place on record
termination order;
[iii]thus, there was no material on record
with regard to date of appointment and/or
termination;
[iv] the claimants alleged that their
services were terminated on and from
30.10.2003 by oral instructions;
[v] whereas in their written statement
(reply), the employer categorically claimed
that service of the claimants were
discontinued in light of circular issued by
the State Government pursuant to GR dated
17.10.1988 and that therefore, the allegation
that the service of the claimants came to be
Page 10
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
terminated in October 2003, is incorrect;
[vi] the employer placed on record document
(muster roll) for various years, last being
1999, on the premise that in subsequent
period, the muster roll do not reflect/bear
names of the claimants.

7. In this view of the matter, before learned
Labour Court there were conflicting claims so far
as date of termination is concerned.
7.1 Even if case of the claimants with regard to
date of appointment and total length of service
rendered by them were to be believed by the
Court, undisputedly, conflicting claims with
regard to date of termination still survived
before learned Labour Court. Under the
circumstances, the learned Labour Court could not
and should not have mechanically accepted the
case of the claimants that their services came to
be terminated in October 2003 more so when the
claimants failed to place on record any material
to demonstrate that their services were
Page 11
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
terminated in October 2003 and that they had
worked after 1999 to 2003.

8. It is pertinent to note that in respect of
the claimants, the employer had placed original
muster roll for certain period on record before
learned Labour Court.
8.1 The details of the attendance of the
claimants which emerged from the muster roll
placed on record by the employer are summarized
in tabular statement by the learned Labour Court
in paragraph No.20 of impugned award.
8.2 When the said details are examined, more
particularly when the remark/ observations by
learned Labour Court with regard to total
attendance of the claimants during each year are
examined, it emerges that the learned Labour
Court itself has recorded, in respect of each
claimant, that from the details emerging from the
muster roll, the claimants had not worked for 240
Page 12
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
days in any phase of 12 months.
8.3 In respect of each claimant, learned Labour
Court has specifically recorded that the
claimants had not completed attendance of 240
days in any year.
8.4 Despite such fact, learned Labour Court, only
on the premise that the employer failed to place
on record muster roll from 1999 to 2003, drew
adverse inference.

9. In view of the fact that even at this stage,
i.e. on record of present petitions, the State
has failed to place any material on record to
convince this Court that the learned Labour Court
has committed any error in drawing adverse
inference, it is not possible for this Court to
hold that the learned Labour Court has committed
any error in drawing adverse inference against
the employer in view of the fact that employer
had failed to place on record document – muster
Page 13
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
roll from 1999 to 2003.
9.1 In this context, it cannot be overlooked that
the employer, undisputedly, did not issue
attendance card to the claimants and/or
appointment order and/or termination order and/or
wage slip. Differently put, the claimants did not
get any document and they had nothing in their
possession which they could have placed on record
to support their case. The attendance register as
well as wage register were in custody of the
employer. The claimants had, during their
deposition, asserted that they worked
continuously and regularly for more than 15 years
and that they had worked for more than 240 days.
9.2 In this view of the matter, the burden to
prove the fact that the claimants had not worked
for 240 days in any year, more particularly in
preceeding 12 months, was on the employer. [See
R.M.Yellati v. Asst. Executive Engineer {(2006) 1
SCC 106} and Shriram Industrial Enterprises Ltd.
Page 14
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
v. Mahak Sinh {(2007) 4 SCC 94].
9.3 In this view of the matter, this Court is not
inclined to interfere with the findings of fact
recorded by learned Labour Court - though on
adverse inference - to the effect that the
claimants had worked for 240 days.

10. Having cleared above mentioned aspect, the
issue which would arise is to ascertain as to
whether the employer followed the procedure
prescribed under Section 25F or not.
10.1 The said provision would be attracted in
present case because it is not the case of the
claimants that service of the claimants were
terminated by way of disciplinary action and/or
upon expiry of specific contract under which the
claimants were engaged for specified period.
10.2 Differently put, it was not the case of the
employer that the termination of the claimants
Page 15
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
fall within any of the three exceptions provided
under Section 2(oo) of the I.D.Act.
10.3 In this view of the matter, the provision
under Section 25F would be attracted which would
oblige the employer to comply the conditions
prescribed under the said provisions viz. to
issue notice and to pay retrenchment compensation
and to follow principle of seniority [Section 25G
and Rule 81 of the Industrial Disputes (Gujarat)
Rules].
10.4 In view of the fact that it was not even
claimed by the employer that such procedure was
followed, it was apparent before the learned
Labour Court that the procedure prescribed by law
was not followed.
10.5 Under the circumstances, the findings by
learned Labour Court that the employer committed
breach of statutory provision cannot be faulted.
Page 16
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER

11. Once this conclusion is reached and it is
found that the decision of learned Labour Court
is just and does not warrant interference, the
only question which would survive is with regard
to appropriate relief.

12. When breach of statutory provision is
established, there is no justification to
interfere with the learned Labour Court's
decision granting reinstatement in service on
original post.

13. However, the issue which deserves
consideration is the direction granting
continuity of service.

14. In this context, it cannot be overlooked and
ignored that the claimants were engaged
irregularly and on ad hoc and daily wage basis.
14.1 The details of attendance recorded by the
learned Labour Court in paragraph No.20 of the
Page 17
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
impugned award go to show that during most of the
period, the claimants had worked for less than
100 days or 150 days in any year. Under the
circumstances, the direction granting continuity
of service is not justified.
14.2 In this context, it is also relevant to keep
in focus that according to the employer, the
arrangement with the claimants was discontinued
in 1999. If that version of the employer is
correct, then, it would mean that the claimants
raised dispute after almost 6 years and in one
case, after almost 10 years. However, since any
cogent material to support the assertion that the
services were terminated in 2003 is not available
on record, this Court would leave the issue at
that stage, more particularly because the learned
Labour Court has accepted workmen's submission.
14.3 Be that as it may. In view of the fact that
the claimants were employed on daily wage and ad
hoc basis, the direction granting continuity of
Page 18
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
service is not justified.
14.4 At the same time, the service rendered by the
claimants prior to date of termination also
cannot be wiped out. Differently put, in peculiar
facts of the case, it is necessary and
appropriate to balance the equity.

15. Having regard to above mentioned aspects and
in light of foregoing discussion, following order
is passed:-
[a] The findings and conclusions by learned
Labour Court that the employer committed breach
of statutory provision while discontinuing
service of the claimants is not disturbed and
said conclusion – decision is confirmed.
[b] The direction granting reinstatement to 9
claimants (i.e. Reference (LCH) Nos. 151 of 2005,
152 of 2005, 153 of 2005, 155 of 2005, 32 of
2006, 33 of 2006, 34 of 2006, 35 of 2006, 41 of
Page 19
C/SCA/4042/2016 ORDER
2006 and 20 of 2009) is also not disturbed and
said direction is also confirmed.
[c] If the State has already not complied
impugned award and has not reinstated the
claimant, then, the competent authority shall
take necessary steps and actions to reinstate the
claimants, as expeditiously as possible, but not
later than four weeks from receipt of this order.
[d] The decision of learned Labour Court refusing
the claim for backwages is not disturbed and said
decision is also confirmed. It is declared that
the claimants shall not be entitled for backwages
from the date of termination until the date of
award.
[e] So far as direction granting continuity of
service is concerned, said direction is partly
set aside and modified. The claimants shall not
be entitled for continuity of service from the
date of termination until the date of award,
Page 20

however, from the date of award their services
shall be considered continuous and their

[f] It is further clarified that only for the
purpose of gratuity, the employer shall take into

[g] Any other or separate direction qua

a few of the pattedars filed Revisions, which were

Learned counsel for the petitioners relying upon the
decision reported in 1987 SC 1353 (Collector, Land
Acquisition, Anantnag and Another v. Mst. Katiji and

condonation of delay should have been considered
sympathetically. Learned counsel for the petitioners

under Section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act contained
enough grounds for condoning the delay and
therefore the delay ought to have been condoned.
Learned Standing Counsel, however, submits that
since there was delay the order was correctly
passed.
Having heard the learned counsel for the petitioners,

1. Both these appeals are filed under Clause 15
of Letters Patent against the order dated
31.07.2018 passed by the learned Single Judge in
Special Civil Application No.19986 of 2016 and
order dated 31.07.2018 passed in Special Civil
Application No.22581 of 2018. By the aforesaid
orders, learned Single Judge has granted interim
relief in favour of the concerned original
petitioners.

2. As the issue involved in both these appeals
Page 1 of 7
C/LPA/1046/2018 ORDER
is interconnected and similar, at the request of
learned advocates appearing for the parties, both
these appeals are heard together. However, for
the sake of convenience, the facts stated in
Special Civil Application No.19986 of 2016 are
considered.

3. Brief facts as stated in Special Civil
Application No.19986 of 2016 are as under:
3.1. It is the case of the original petitioner
that in a meeting dated 03.08.2016 of the
Executive Body of the petitioner society,
unanimous resolution was passed to hold the
election of the petitioner society and so far as
the primary voters’ list is concerned, no change
is to be made in the primary voters’ list already
prepared for the election of previous Executive
Body. However, the original respondent No.4 i.e.
the present appellant has filed Lavad Suit No.154
of 2016 in the Board of Nominees Court, Mahesana
for declaration and injunction on 10.08.2016. In
the said Lavad Suit, the appellant herein sought
injunction against the petitioner society that
without publishing primary voters’ list, the
Election Officer be restrained from proceeding
with the election process. In the said suit, the
Board of Nominees passed an ex parte order below
the temporary injunction application whereby the
petitioner society and the Election Officer were
restrained from proceeding with the election
process without publishing the primary voters’
Page 2 of 7
C/LPA/1046/2018 ORDER
list till 22.08.2016. It is stated that primary
voters’ list was published and election was held
on 20.08.2016 and new committee has taken over
the charge. However, original respondent No.1
passed an order dated 08.09.2016 under the
provisions of Section 74(D) of the Gujarat
Cooperative Societies Act (hereinafter referred
to as ‘the Act’ for short) and appointed a
custodian. The petitioner, thereafter, filed
Revision Application No.262 of 2016 before the
original respondent No.3, wherein the respondent
No.3 passed an order dated 24.10.2016 by which
the interim relief granted earlier in favour of
the petitioner is vacated. The petitioner has,
therefore, filed the captioned petition
challenging both the aforesaid orders. Petition
is thereafter amended and the order of extension
of terms of the custodian is also challenged
subsequently.

4. The learned Single Judge, by the impugned
order, granted interim relief in favour of the
original petitioner. The appellant – original
respondent No.4 has, therefore, filed both these
appeals.

5. Heard learned advocate Mr. Dilip B. Rana for
the appellants, learned advocate Mr. Dipen Desai
for the respondents – original petitioners and
learned Assistant Government Pleader for the
respondent authorities.
Page 3 of 7
C/LPA/1046/2018 ORDER

6. Learned advocate Mr. Rana mainly contended
that though the order of injunction was in
operation till 22.08.2016, the election was held
on 20.08.2016 and thereby the original petitioner
has violated the order of injunction and
conducted the election. It is submitted that in
the Revision Application filed by the petitioner
the stay granted earlier was vacated by the
respondent No.3. It is submitted that the learned
Single Judge has granted interim relief by which
practically the principal relief is allowed which
is not permissible. In support of the said
contention, learned advocate has placed reliance
upon the decision rendered by the Division Bench
of this Court in the case of Union of India,
Ministry of Chemicals and Ferti. v. Ambalal
Sarabhai Enterprises Ltd. and Ors., reported in
2010(3) GLH 689. It is, therefore, urged that the
impugned order be set aside.

7. On the other hand, learned advocate Mr. Dipen
Desai appearing for the original petitioner
submitted that the petitioner has not violated
the order of injunction granted by the Board of
Nominees. It is submitted that primary voters’
list was published and thereafter election was
held. It is submitted that the respondent No.1
could not have exercised the powers for
appointment of custodian under Section 74(D) of
the Act in case of election dispute. Election
dispute is not covered within Section 74(D) of
the Act. By appointing the custodian, the
Page 4 of 7
C/LPA/1046/2018 ORDER
election of members of the petitioner society is
indirectly set aside without the same is
challenged before the competent forum. It is
submitted that the present case is squarely
covered by the decision rendered by the Division
Bench of this Court rendered on 22.11.2017 in
Letters Patent Appeal No.204 of 2017 and allied
matters. It is contended that learned Single
Judge has not committed any error while granting
interim relief in favour of the original
petitioner and therefore this appeal be
dismissed.

8. Having considered the submissions canvassed
by the learned advocates appearing for the
parties and having gone through the material
produced on record, it transpires that the Board
of Nominees has though granted injunction the
same was conditional one and it is the case of
the original petitioner that after publication of
the primary voters’ list the election was held on
20.08.2016 after publication of primary voters’
list. The fact remains that the election of the
petitioner society is held and election of the
members of the said society is not challenged
till date. We have also gone through the decision
dated 22.11.2017 rendered by the Division Bench
of this Court in Letters Patent Appeal No.204 of
2017 and allied matters. We are of the view that
the learned Single Judge has not committed any
error while placing reliance upon the said
decision while granting interim relief in favour
Page 5 of 7
C/LPA/1046/2018 ORDER
of the original petitioner. Whether the
respondent No.1 has power to appoint a custodian
while exercising the powers under Section 74(D)
of the Act or not is to be decided by the learned
Single Judge. However, prima facie, when the
learned Single Judge found that no stay has been
granted on the election of elected members of the
petitioner society and therefore holding of
election by the petitioner itself is not a ground
to appoint custodian under Section 74(D) of the
Act, we see no reason to interfere with the
impugned order passed by the learned Single
Judge.

9. The decision rendered by the Division Bench
of this Court in the case of Union of India,
Ministry of Chemicals and Ferti (supra) upon
which reliance is placed by the learned advocate
appearing for the appellant would not render any
assistance to him. In the said case, it was
observed by the Hon’ble Division Bench that in a
matter of public revenue ordinarily stay should
not be granted in absence of extraordinary
circumstances. However, facts of the present case
are different.

10. It is also required to be noted that the
learned Single Judge has directed the respondent
No.3 to expedite the hearing of Revision
Application No.292 of 2016 and decide the same as
Page 6 of 7
C/LPA/1046/2018 ORDER
expeditiously as possible, but not later than one
month from the date of receipt of the said order.
In that view of the matter also, we are not
inclined to entertain these appeals. Accordingly,
appeals are dismissed. Consequently, all
connected civil applications stand disposed of.

ORDER
The appellant is the complainant in S.T. No. 2281
of 2013 on the files of the court below. The appellant
filed a complaint against the first respondent herein
before the court below alleging offence under Section
138 of the N.I.Act. On 8-12-2017, the appellant was
not present before the court below. In the said
circumstances, the court below acquitted the accused
under Section 256 (1) Cr.P.C., against which this Appeal
has been filed after obtaining Special Leave from this
Court.
2. Heard.

3. It has been submitted by the learned counsel
for the appellant that on 8-12-2017, the appellant could
-2-
Crl. Appeal No. 224 of 2018
not appear before the court below on the reason that the
appellant was laid up. However, a petition to condone
her absence was filed before the court below on that day.
But, the court below, without considering that application,
acquitted the accused under Section 256 (1) Cr.P.C. The
above submission of the learned counsel for the
appellant finds place in the memorandum of appeal as
well.

4. It is not discernible from the order impugned
as to whether the appellant was represented before the
court below on 8-12-2017 or not. Since it was not
recorded that the complainant was not represented on
8-12-2017, it has to be inferred that the complainant
was duly represented before the court below on
8-12-2017. It is also not discernible from the order
impugned as to whether any application was filed to
condone the absence of the appellant before the court on
8-12-2017. The certified copy of the petition, filed on
behalf of the appellant to condone the absence of the
appellant before the court below on 8-12-2017, has
-3-
Crl. Appeal No. 224 of 2018
been produced before this Court by the learned counsel
for the appellant, for my perusal. The certified copy
will form part of the records of this court. It is seen from
the said certified copy that the same was filed before the
court below on 8-12-2017 itself and the learned
Magistrate rejected the same without assigning any
reason.

5. Since an application had been filed on behalf
of the appellant before the court below to condone the
absence of the appellant on 8-12-2017 stating that the
appellant was laid up, the court below ought not have
axed down the complaint at the threshold under Section
256 (1) Cr.P.C. For the said reason, the order impugned
can not be said to be legal, proper and correct.
Consequently, I set aside the same.
In the result, this appeal stands allowed, setting
aside order dated 8-12-2017 in S.T. 2281 of 2013 passed
by the court below acquitting the accused under Section
256 (1) Cr.P.C. and the court below is directed to proceed
-4-
Crl. Appeal No. 224 of 2018
with in accordance with law. The proceedings of the
court below shall stand relegated to the stage prior to the
acquittal of the accused by the court below on 8-12-
2017.
The parties shall appear before the trial Court on
25-4-2018 without further notice.
