APPLICATION U/S 482 BNSS No. - 4894 of 2025
Applicant :- Meera
Opposite Party :- State of U.P.
Counsel for Applicant :- Vikas Yadav,Vishveshwar Mani Tripathi
Counsel for Opposite Party :- G.A.
Hon'ble Vivek Varma,J.

1. Supplementary affidavit filed by counsel for the applicant is
taken on record.

2. Heard counsel for the applicant and Sri P.K. Tripathi, learned
A.G.A. for the State- opposite party, and perused the material
placed on record.

3. This application has been filed seeking anticipatory bail in Case
Crime No.241 of 2024, under Sections 191(2), 115(2), 351(2),
117(2), 109 B.N.S., Police Station -Maeel, District -Deoria.

4. Counsel for the applicant submits that the applicant has been
falsely implicated in the present case. As per the first information
report, the applicant along with six others are alleged to have
assaulted five persons, namely Arvind (informant), Roshan,
Ranjeet, Rajendra and Meenu. No medical report with regard to
Roshan and Ranjeet is available in the case diary. Meenu received
four injuries, which were simple in nature. Rajendra received six
injuries, which were simple in nature, except injury no.2. The
injury no.2 was referred for x-ray. As per the report of radiologist,
fracture of ring finger of left hand was seen. As per the medical
report of Arvind, he received four injuries. Injury no.1 was referred
for C.T. Scan. As per the report of doctor, fracture on the skull
region was found. In the statement of the injured Arvind, co-
accused Roshan was alleged to have caused injury on his head. A
vague and general role has been assigned to the applicant. The
applicant has not been nominated as the principal offender, who
caused injury on the head of Arvind and injury no.2 to Rajendra.
The case of the applicant is clearly distinguishable from that of
aforesaid co-accused. At this stage, there is no credible evidence to
link the applicant with the offence. The applicant is a lady and has
no criminal antecedents. It is next submitted that the investigation
is going on and the applicant has apprehension of her arrest in the
above mentioned case.

5. Learned A.G.A. has opposed the prayer for anticipatory bail but
could not satisfactorily dispute the aforesaid submissions from the
record.

6. Counsel for the applicant further submits that the application for
grant of anticipatory bail be confined only till the submission of
police report.

7. Having regard to the submissions made, considering the nature
of accusations, antecedents of the applicant and the fact that a
vague and general role has been assigned to the applicant; the
applicant has not been nominated as the principal offender, who
caused injury on the head of Arvind and injury no.2 to Rajendra;
at this stage, there is no substantive evidence to link the applicant
with the offence; without commenting on merits of the case, I am
of the opinion that the applicant is entitled to be enlarged on
anticipatory bail till the submission of police report.

8. In the event of arrest, the applicant- Meera be released on
anticipatory bail in the aforesaid case crime till the submission of
police report, if any, under Section 193(3) B.N.S.S., on furnishing
a personal bond of Rs. 50,000/- with two sureties each in the like
amount to the satisfaction of the Station House Officer of the
police station concerned with the following conditions:-
(i) The applicant shall make herself available for interrogation by a
police officer as and when required;
(ii) The applicant shall not directly or indirectly make any
inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the
facts of the case so as to dissuade from disclosing such facts to the
Court or to any police officer;
(iii) The applicant shall not leave India without the previous
permission of the Court and if she has passport, the same shall be
deposited by her, before the S.S.P./S.P. concerned.

9. In default of any of the conditions, the Investigating Officer is at
liberty to file appropriate application for cancellation of
anticipatory bail granted to the applicant.

10. The Investigating Officer is directed to conclude the
investigation of the present case in accordance with law
expeditiously preferably within a period of three months from the
date of production of a copy of this order independently without
being prejudiced by any observation made by this Court while
considering and deciding the present anticipatory bail application
of the applicant.

11. The applicant is directed to produce a copy of this order before
the S.S.P./S.P. concerned within ten days from today, who shall
ensure the compliance of present order.

12. The application stands disposed of.

Hon'ble Pankaj Bhatia,J.
Heard counsel for the petitioner, Sri Deo Dayal,
counsel appearing on behalf of the Respondents
No. 2 and 3 and perused the record.
The present writ has been filed alleging that the
husband of the petitioner was appointed as
Assistant Teacher in the primary school died on
14.5.2002 while in service. The petitioner claims
appointing under the Dying-in-Harness Rules,
however, no decision was taken, as such, the
petitioner approached this Court by filing a Writ
Petition No. 15186 of 2008, which was disposed
off vide order dated 29.3.2008 directing the
respondents to take a decision within the time
frame as fixed by this Court. It is argued that in
compliance of the order of this Court,
Respondent No. 2 moved a letter before the
Respondent No. 3 asking for relevant documents
of the petitioner so that decision may be taken. In
terms thereof, Respondent No. 3 proceeded to
pass an order on 20.5.2010 recording that as the
matter is awaiting direction from the office of
Respondent No. 2, no decision can be taken for
appointment. The said order was passed on
20.5.2010. Thus, the petitioner has approached
this Court seeking a direction upon the
Respondent No. 2 to grant appointment under the
Dying-in-Harness Rules.
The facts, as emerge, that the husband of the
petitioner died in the year 2002 and the disposal
of the application was done in the year 2010. It is
well settled that the intent and purpose of the
Dying-in-Harness Rules is to tide over the
immediate financial crises faced by the
petitioner's family.
Considering the fact that the husband of the
petitioner died in the year 2002, the issuance of
mandamus after 19 years is against the intent and
purpose of Dying-in-Harness Rules, as such, no
case for issuance of mandamus is made out.
The writ petition is dismissed.
Copy of the order downloaded from the official
website of this Court shall be treated as certified
copy of the order.

The aforecaptioned Review Petition has been filed seeking to review
and recall the impugned judgment dated 4.12.2018 rendered by this Court
in W.P.(C.) No.39284 of 2018 filed by the R1 herein (writ petitioner). The
review petition has been filed by the 4th respondent in the W.P.(C.).

2. This Court had dispensed with notice to R4 in the W.P.(C.) and
had passed the impugned judgment on 4.12.2018 in the above W.P.(C.)
No. 39284 of 2018, wherein it has been inter alia ordered that the refusal
on the part of the respondents 2 and 3 therein in accepting basic land tax
from the writ petitioner merely on the ground of pendency of the regular
second appeal or any such other civil proceedings by itself will not amount
to any legal bar to accept basic land tax. Accordingly, this Court ordered the
competent authority among respondents 2 and 3 in the W.P.(C) more
particularly, 3rd respondent therein should forthwith accept basic land tax
from the writ petitioner and issue land tax receipt to him immediately on
production of a certified copy of this order. So also, it is made clear that in
case, the writ petitioner makes any application for possession
RP.No.850 OF 2019 3
certificate/location sketch etc, then also the 3rd respondent in W.P.(C.) shall
consider and grant the same and cannot refuse the same on the sole ground
of pendency of the RSA.

3. Now, the main ground urged by the review petitioner (R4 in the
W.P.(C.)) is to the effect that though review petitioner could not succeed in
the original suit O.S.No.184/2010 on the file of the Munsiff Court, Kalpetta
which was filed by the writ petitioner, in which the review petitioner has
been arrayed as the defendant therein, the review petitioner had later filed
a first appeal which culminated in Ext.P2 judgment, which is also adverse
to the review petitioner. Thereafter, the review petitioner has filed regular
second appeal as RSA No.529/2018 which is pending before this Court.

4. It has already been made clear by this Court in para No.4 of the
impugned judgment in this W.P.(C.) that it is well settled by various rulings
of this Court as in Sudan v.State of Kerala [2013 (4) KLT 563] that
mere pendency of the any civil suit cannot be a legal bar in accepting basic
land tax unless the same is legally restrained or interdicted by the
competent court. Further that, it has also been held in decisions as in
Vijayarajan v. Tahsildar [2013 (2) KLT SN 93] that pendency of civil
suit is not a ground for non-acceptance of land tax and that attachment of
the property by the revenue recovery officials etc. also result in non-
acceptance of land tax and that it has also been held in decisions as in
Sawarni v. Inder Kaur and others [AIR 1996 SC 2823] by the Apex
RP.No.850 OF 2019 4
Court that data mutation by itself does not create or extinguish the title
nor has it any presumptive value on title and it only enables the person in
whose favour mutation is ordered to pay the land tax to the authorities
concerned. The abovesaid legal position is also explicitly incorporated in
Rule 16 of the Transfer of Registry Rules, 1966 which stipulates that
summary enquiry and decision thereon on the issue of mutation is only an
arrangement for fiscal purposes and does not affect the legal rights of any
person in respect of lands covered by the decisions in transfer of registry
cases and that the question of legal rights will always subject to
adjudication by Civil Courts and pattas will be revised from time to time in
accordance with the judicial decisions.

5. Accordingly, it is made clear that the decision of the competent
revenue authorities to accept basic land tax from the writ petitioner or to
issue land tax receipt to him or to issue possession certificate/location
sketch etc. in respect of the subject property will be subject to the final
result in the regular second appeal RSA No.539/2018 now on the file of this
Court. It is further made clear that in case the review petitioner could
succeed in the said regular second appeal and if the findings and directions
in the said judgment are pertinent and relevant for the present purpose of
deciding as to from whom the basic land tax is to be accepted etc., then the
review petitioner will be at liberty to file a appropriate application before
the respondent-Tahsildar concerned as conceived in Rule 16 of the Transfer
RP.No.850 OF 2019 5
of Registry Rules,1966 along with the certified copy of the said judgment
seeking for revision of the decision regarding mutation and acceptance of
the basic land tax made in favour of the writ petitioner and to contend that
such revision is so warranted on account of such judicial verdict in the civil
proceedings and then in such a case, the Tahsildar shall consider and pass
orders on such petition, after hearing both sides. No further clarification or
orders are required in this case.
With these observations and directions, the above review petition will
stand finally disposed of.

4. In this factual background, learned counsel for the petitioners,
Mr. Gurmohan Singh Bedi, has contended that grave prejudice has been caused
to the petitioners by the impugned orders whereby the E.D., which is stranger
to the complaints, has been permitted to inspect the records/Court file and use
the same for investigation against them. It is further contended that the records
contain secret information given by the French Republic to the Government of
India and there is a specific bar on providing any such information to a stranger
under the “Agreement for Avoidance of Double Taxation with France”. It has
been entered into between the Government of India and the Government of
French Republic for avoidance of double taxation and prevention of fiscal
evasion with respect to taxes on income and capital, and has come in force on
01.08.1994. He has specifically relied upon Article 28 of Convention to the
Agreement notified on 07.09.1994 and amended on 12.08.2009, which reads as

(2) In no case shall the provisions of paragraph 1 be construed

Contracting State ;

5. Per contra, Mr. Zoheb Hossain, learned Special Counsel for the
respondents, contend that the order is well-reasoned and cannot cause any
prejudice to the petitioner, as the E.D. has only been allowed to access judicial
documents. Besides, Rule 2 of Part-C, Chapter 16, of the Punjab and Haryana
High Court Rules and Orders, Volume 4, specifically allows even a stranger to
inspect the Court record for sufficient reasons. The revisional Court has taken
that into consideration, and finding sufficient reasons in the E.D.’s application
for inspection of records, allowed the same which is in accordance with law.
He further contended that in Ram Jethmalani and others v. Union of India and
others, (2011) 8 SCC 1, an article similar to Article 28 has been examined and
interpreted by the Supreme Court holding that it is not a restrain on disclosing
the information.

Department against the petitioners under Section 277 of the Income Tax Act,
1961, read with Section 176, 177, 181, 186, 187, 193 and 199 of the IPC,
wherein information in the form of master sheets originally received in Paris,
France, by the competent authority of India/Foreign Tax and Tax Research
Division of Central Board of Direct Taxes from the competent French authority,
has been placed on record. It is to the effect that the petitioners are ‘beneficiaries

of foreign assets maintained and controlled through foreign business entities’.
During pendency of proceedings before the Magistrate, the E.D. moved an
application for inspection of the aforesaid information/documents on the
ground that it was also seized of the subject matter of the complaint, and for the
purpose of conducting investigation the documents were required to be
examined. The application was allowed vide impugned order dated 18.09.2020,
and revision petition against the same was dismissed vide impugned order dated
02.09.2021. While dismissing the revision petition, learned Additional Sessions
Judge referred to Rule 2 of Part-C, Chapter 16 of the Punjab and Haryana High
Court Rules and Orders, Volume 4, which allowed even a stranger to a civil or
a criminal case to inspect record of pending case(s) for sufficient reasons. The
reasons for inspection of record put forth by the E.D. were found sufficient, and
the E.D. was allowed to inspect the file, by recording as under:

of Punjab and Haryana High Court relevant to the issue are

[Provided that a stranger to a civil or criminal case

8. Further, learned counsel for the petitioners has assailed the
impugned orders permitting inspection of the records on the ground that in
Article 28 of the Convention under the “Agreement for Avoidance of Double
Taxation with France” entered into between the Government of India and the
French Republic, there is a bar on disclosing any information received by the
contracting State and it is to be treated as secret under the domestic law. And
as provided therein, it can only be disclosed to the persons or authorities
CRM-M-37200-2021 with two connected matters -10-
involved in the assessment or collection of taxes or enforcement or prosecution
thereof, etc. However, it remains undisputed that the information or documents
placed on record before the Magistrate by the I.T. Department have been
received by it in the French Republic at Paris, and its use as well as
dissemination is regulated under the Agreement for Avoidance of Double
Taxation, referred to above. The Supreme Court in Ram Jethmalani case
(supra) had the occasion to examine one such Avoidance of Double Taxation
Agreement entered into between the Government of India and Germany; Article
26 of the said agreement was pari materia to Article 28 of the Agreement in
question. The Court examined the issue, whether the article proscribed
disclosing of information received by the Government of India under the
Agreement, and also whether in the context of proceedings under Article 32 of
the Constitution the Union of India could claim exemption from providing such
information to the petitioners. The Court held as under:
67. Relevant portions of Article 26 of the double taxation agreement
with Germany, a copy of which was submitted by the Union of India,
reads as follows:
“26. Exchange of information.—(1) The competent
authorities of the contracting States shall exchange such
information as is necessary for carrying out the purposes of
this agreement. Any information received by a contracting
State shall be treated as secret in the same manner as
information obtained under the domestic laws of that State and
shall be disclosed only to persons or authorities (including
courts and administrative bodies) involved in the assessment
or collection of, the enforcement or prosecution in respect of,
or the determination of appeals in relation to, the taxes covered
by this agreement. They may disclose the information in
public court proceedings or in judicial proceedings.

The E.D. is permitted to inspect the record of the complaints before the
Magistrate and access the information/documents; however, the same shall not
be disseminated publicly unless permitted in accordance with law.

Even the case is taken up in revised call no one has appeared on

Heard Sri Aniruddha Kumar Singh, the learned A.G.A.-I for the State-
appellant and perused the material available on record.
The present appeal under Section 378 Cr.P.C. has been filed against
the judgment and order dated 02.02.2007 passed by learned
Additional District and Sessions Judge/ F.T.C.-II, Room No. 11,
District Sultanpur in Session Trial No. 423 of 1999, State Vs. Rakesh
Tiwari and another, arising out of Case Crime No. 478 of 1997, under
Sections 308, 452, 323, 504, 506 I.P.C., Police Station Gosaiganj,
District Sultanpur, releasing the opposite parties under Section 360
Cr.P.C. on a personal bond and surety of Rs. 10,000/-.
As per the prosecution version on 07.12.1997 at about 3:30 p.m.
when the complainant was coming dragging his trolley loaded with
boulders, an altercation took place, on account of which accused
persons came at the house of complainant and started abusing him,
when the complainant objected then the accused persons assaulted
him with lathi-danda holding in their hands. In the said incident the
complainant and his other family members sustained injuries. On the
basis of above report a case was got registered against all the accused
persons and the case was investigated, and after investigation charge
sheet was filed against all the accused persons. All the accused were
charged under Sections 308, 452, 323, 504, 506, they pleaded not
guilty and claimed to be tried.
The court below after taking into consideration the facts and
circumstances of the case and evidence available on record, passed
the judgment and order of acquittal dated 02.02.2007.
Learned A.G.A.-I for the State-appellant submits that the court below
did not appreciate the evidence on record. He further submits that
prosecution has successfully proved the offence against the accused on
the basis of evidence. The judgment was passed without considering
the statement of witnesses and the case set up by the prosecution and
the judgment of the acquittal was passed on surmises and conjectures.
2
The present appeal is of the year, 2007. Moreover, there appears no
illegality or infirmity in the judgment and order of acquittal passed by
the court below.

HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE FARJAND ALI
Order
22/04/2024
1. By way of filing the instant misc. petition challenge has been
made to the order dated 31.01.2023 whereby the learned Judicial
Magistrate, No.02, Pali it is ordered to get comparison of the thumb
impression of the petitioner with the thumb impression available on
the application form for allotment of license.
2. Bereft of elaborate details succinctly stated the fact of the case
are that a complaint came to be submitted against the petitioner
alleging inter-alia that for the purpose of obtaining a liquor license an
application got moved in the office of excise department. The
complainant had alleged that though the application was moved in
the name of the petitioner but the thumb impression appended on
that application did not belong to her. An application was moved by
the complainant probably in the month of January 2016 making a
prayer for sending the disputed document to FSL for the purpose of
examination of thumb impression on the disputed and undisputed
[2024:RJ-JD:17423] (2 of 3) [CRLMP-44/2024]
document. Vide order dated 06.01.2016 the learned Magistrate had
rejected the prayer for the reason that an application under Section
311A Cr.P.C. was not maintainable owing to the reason that neither
the accused was not arrested nor was he in custody. After around 12
months again the same nature of application got submitted by the
same complainant. To the utter dismay, the said application had been
kept pending by the learned Magistrate for long seven years. Vide
the order dated 31.01.2023 the learned Magistrate has allowed the
application preferred on behalf of the complainant and now directed
to send the disputed thumb impression of the petitioner along with
undisputed thumb impression to the handwriting expert for its
comparison.

3. I am of the view that when a question has been determined by
a criminal Court finally then the same issue cannot be re-agitated at
a subsequent stage. A criminal Court becomes functus officio after
passing any order on any question and either question of law or
question of fact. Section 362 Cr.P.C. makes it abundantly clear that
except the arithmetical and clerical error an order cannot be revisited
in a criminal proceeding.

4. In this view of the matter, the misc. petition is allowed. The
orders under challenge dated 31.01.2023 passed by learned Judicial
Magistrate, No.02, Pali and order dated 17.11.2023 passed by
learned Additional Sessions Judge, Pali are hereby quashed and set
aside. Learned Magistrate is directed to conclude the judicial
proceeding pending before him within a period of 40 days after
receipt of a copy of this order.

5. Accordingly, the instant misc. petition as well as stay petition is
disposed of.
[2024:RJ-JD:17423] (3 of 3) [CRLMP-44/2024]

6. An explanation shall also be forwarded to this Court as to
why proceeding of a criminal complaint like this had been kept
pending in the Court for long seven to eight years.
(FARJAND ALI),J

Petitioner seeks implementation of the order of the Andhra Pradesh
Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad (hereinafter referred to as ‘the
Tribunal’) directing refund of the amount which had been withheld on
the score that such sum was wrongfully paid to the petitioner on the
scale of pay with Language Pandit Grade-I.
This issue is no longer res integra in view of the decision of the Full
Bench of this Court in Writ Petition No.21457 of 2004 and batch,
wherein after examining the provisions of Act 1 of 2005, the Bench had
inter alia held as follows:
“(iii) The impugned Act is silent with regard to recovery of
the amounts already paid to those Grade-II Pandits who availed
the benefit under G.O.Ms.No.330, dated 10.08.1983 and hence
the Government shall not recover any amount actually and
already paid to any of the Language Pandits Grade-II who were
given benefit of Scale of Pay of Grade-I”
The aforesaid decision was followed by a coordinate Bench of this
Court in Writ Petition No.33315 of 2013 dated 22.06.2020.
Petitioner is also a Language Pandit, who had been given the
benefit of scale of pay of Grade-I. Hence, the amount already paid
2

the ration in the aforesaid decisions. Thus, the Tribunal passed
order, dated 26.11.2012 directing refund of the amount
recovered/withheld from the retiral benefits of the petitioner. Such
order has not been implemented as yet.
Since the issue is no longer res integra in the light of the
aforesaid decisions, the order ought to be forthwith implemented.

wrongfully recovered/withheld from the pensionary benefits within
eight (8) weeks from date, failing which, the said amount shall carry

1. The petitioner made a complaint against respondent No.2 for
commission of offence under Sections 294, 506 Part-II and 494 of the
IPC. Concerned police station investigated the offence and submitted the
charge-sheet against respondent No.2 and in turn, the trial Court framed
the charges for offence under Sections 294, 506 Part-II and 494 of the
IPC. However, the revisional Court by order dated 24.1.2017 discharged
respondent No.2 for offence under Section 494 of the IPC in view of bar
contained in Section 198(1) (c) of the CrPC, against which, this petition
under Section 482 of the CrPC has been filed.
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner would submit that the
impugned order is bad and unsustainable in law.
3. I have heard learned counsel for the petitioner.

4. Section 198(1) (c) of the CrPC clearly stipulates that no Court
shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under Chapter XX
including Section 494 of the IPC except upon a complaint made by some
person aggrieved by the offence.

5. In view of that, only on the complaint filed by aggrieved person
before the Magistrate, cognizance can be taken. The police has no
authority and jurisdiction to take cognizance for offence under Section
494 of the IPC on the report made by aggrieved person, therefore, the
order of the revisional Court is absolutely sustainable and no interference
is called for.

6. Accordingly, the petition is dismissed. However, the petitioner is
at liberty to proceed in accordance with law.

This Criminal Miscellaneous Case is filed under
Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
(“the Code” for the sake of brevity).

2. Petitioner was originally the 7th accused in
C.C.No.472/2006 on the file of the Judicial First Class
Magistrate Court - II, Attingal arising from Crime
No.89/2006 of Venjaramoodu Police Station which is
now pending as C.C.No.1718/2018 before the same
court.

3. It is submitted that the petitioner was not
able to appear before the trial court and his case was
Crl.M.C.No.8188 of 2023
3
split up and the case against the other accused were
continued and the other accused were acquitted as
per Annexure-2 judgment.

4. Heard counsel for the petitioner and the
Public Prosecutor. The counsel for the petitioner
submitted that the co-accused were already acquitted
by the trial court and the continuation of the trial
against the petitioner will be an abuse of process of
court because the substratum of the prosecution case
is shattered. The Public Prosecutor submitted that the
petitioner has to face trial before the lower court and
this court may not invoke the powers under Section
482 of the Code.

5. This Court in Moosa v. Sub Inspector of
Police (2006 (1) KLT 552), Abbas T.K. v. State
of Kerala (2013 KHC 336) and in Ashraf
Kancheriyil v. State of Kerala (2011(2) KHC
Crl.M.C.No.8188 of 2023
4
812) considered the powers of this court to invoke
Section 482 of the Code to quash the proceedings
based on the acquittal of co-accused. The dictum laid
down by this court in the above judgment is that, if
substratum of prosecution case is shattered by the
judgement of acquittal of the co-accused that could
be taken into account while considering the request
to quash the proceedings. After going through the
judgment of the trial court, I am of the considered
opinion that the continuation of the prosecution
against the petitioner will be an abuse of process of
court. It will be beneficial to extract the relevant
portion of Annexure-2 judgment by which the co-
accused were acquitted:
“6. Point No.1:- As stated earlier, the presence
of CW1 to CW3 could not be secured even after
resorting to coercive steps. Hence they are dispensed
with. Examination of other witnesses were given up
by the prosecution. As there was no incriminating
Crl.M.C.No.8188 of 2023
5
evidence against the accused, 313(1)(b) examination
was also dispensed with. The prosecution has failed
to prove the case. Hence, the point No.1 is answered
against the prosecution.

7. Point No.2:- From my discussions to point
No.1, I hold that the accused Nos.4,6 and 9 are
innocent of the charges levelled against them.
So,they are to be acquitted.

8. In the result, accused Nos.4,6 and 9 are
acquitted u/s.248(1) Cr.P.C. They are set at liberty
and their bail bonds will stand cancelled. Case
against Al to 3, 5, 7,8 and 10 is refiled as CC
905/2011.”
From the above, it is clear that the substratum
of the prosecution case is shattered by the judgment
delivered by the lower court, while acquitting the co-
accused. Therefore, this court is of the view that the
continuation of the prosecution will be an abuse of
process of court and it will be a judicial waste of time.
Therefore, this Crl.M.C can be allowed.
Therefore, this Criminal Miscellaneous case is
Crl.M.C.No.8188 of 2023
6
allowed. All further proceedings against the
petitioner in C.C.No.1718/2018 on the file of the
Judicial First Class Magistrate Court - II, Attingal
arising from Crime No.89/2006 of Venjaramoodu
Police Station are quashed.

The petitioner was appointed as Tax
Inspector prior to the year 1988. He was
granted regular pay scale on 01.05.1994.
The employer has also revised the pay
scale on the basis of the recommendation
of Sixth Pay Commission on 17.10.2008.
However, order dated 04.01.2017 has been
issued, whereby recovery of Rs.11,35,439/-
has been ordered.
The petitioner started getting
regular pay scale w.e.f. 01.05.1994. He was
given benefit of Sixth Pay Commission on
17.10.2008.
The petitioner has never misled or
misrepresented the facts that he was
granted regular pay scale to the post of Tax
Inspector on 01.05.1994 and benefit of the
Sixth Pay Commission on 17.10.2008. The
petitioner has been discharging his duties
since 1988. The petitioner belongs to the
lower strata of the society.
Their Lordships of the Honíble
Supreme Court in (2015) 4 SCC 334 in the
case of State of Punjab and others Vs.
Rafiq Masih (White Washer) and other
analogous petitions have held as under:-

18. It is not possible to postulate all
situations of hardship, which would govern
employees on the issue of recovery, where
payments have mistakenly been made by the
employer, in excess of their entitlement. Be
that as it may, based on the decision referred
to herein above, we may, as a ready reference,
summarise the following few situations,
wherein recoveries by the employers, would be
impermissible in law:
(i) Recovery from employees belonging
to Class-III and Class-IV service (Or Group C
and Group D service).
(ii) Recovery from the retired employees,
or the employees who are due to retire within
one year, of the order of recovery.
(iii) Recovery from the employees, when
the excess payment has been made for a
period of excess of five years, before the order
of recovery is issued.
(iv) Recovery in case where an employee
has wrongfully been required to discharge
duties of a higher post, and has been paid
accordingly, even though he should have
rightfully been required to work against an
inferior post.
(v) In any other cases, where the court
arrives at the conclusion, that recovery if
made from the employee, would be iniquitous
of harsh or arbitrary to such an extent, as
would far outweigh the equitable balance of
the employerís right to recover.
The petitioner has also worked in
Class III post, thus, it would be
impermissible as per the law laid down by
their Lordships of the Honíble Supreme
Court to recover the amount, which has
already been paid to the petitioner.
It is not one of those cases, where the
pay scale has been granted by mistake. The
employer has paid a regular pay scale on
01.05.1994 and revised on 17.10.2008.
Accordingly, the writ petition is
allowed. Letter dated 04.01.2017 is quashed
and set aside.

(Ujjal Bhuyan, J)
This case was heard on 23.02.2018 and fixed for delivery of order on 26.03.2018
but as the Bench was not available, delivery of order was deferred to 27.03.2018.

2. Heard Mr. A. T. Sarkar, learned counsel for the petitioner and Mr. A. Kalita, learned
Special Counsel, Foreigners Tribunal (FT).

3. By filing this petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, petitioner seeks
quashing of order dated 30.08.2016 passed by the Foreigners Tribunal, Barpeta 11th at Sorbhog
in FT Case No. 76/2015
(Union of India Vs Hanif Ali @ Hanifuddin) declaring the petitioner to
be a foreigner who had illegally entered into India (Assam) from Bangladesh after 25.03.1971.

4. This Court by order dated 08.11.2016 had issued notice while requisitioning the case
record and passed an interim order to the effect that petitioner shall be allowed to remain on
bail subject to his appearance before the Superintendent of Police (Border), Barpeta and
furnishing of adequate surety.

5. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties have been considered. Also
perused the materials on record, including the record requisitioned from the Tribunal.

6. Record discloses that Election Commission of India had ordered intensive revision
of electoral rolls for the Sorbhog Assembly Constituency in the State of Assam with reference to
01.01.1997 as the qualifying date. In this connection, a house to house enumeration was carried
out during the period from 16.01.1997 to 15.04.1997. Though the name of the petitioner was
included in the draft electoral rolls of the said Constituency published on 24.07.1997, Electoral
Page No.# 3/6
Registration Officer of the said Constituency expressed doubts about the citizenship of the
petitioner and got the matter verified by an on the spot local verification. On consideration of
the report of such verification, Electoral Registration Officer expressed reasonable doubt that
the petitioner was not a citizen of India. Thereafter matter was forwarded to the
Superintendent of Police (Border), Barpeta who after complying with the required formalities
made the reference under the
Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983 (IMDT
Act) suspecting the petitioner to be an illegal migrant as defined under IMDT Act. Be it stated
that under Section 3 (1)(c) of the IMDT Act, an illegal migrant was defined as a foreigner who
had unauthorisedly entered into India after 25.03.1971. The said reference was registered as
IMDT Case No. 3865/B/1998 before the Illegal Migrants (Determination) Tribunal, Barpeta.

7. In the meanwhile, IMDT Act was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in
Sarbananda Sonowal Vs Union of India reported in
(2005) 5 SCC 665 with the further
direction that those references which were pending before the Tribunals constituted under the
IMDT Act should be transferred to the Tribunals constituted under the
Foreigners’ Act, 1946
read with the
Foreigners’ (Tribunals) Order, 1964. The related reference was thereafter
registered as FT (II) Case No. 4438/2012 before the Foreigners Tribunal No. 2, Barpeta. After
creation of additional Tribunals, the reference was assigned to the Foreigners’ Tribunal No. 11th,
Barpeta at Sorbhog (Tribunal) where it was re-numbered as FT Case No. 76/2015.

8. In his written statement filed on 08.02.2016 petitioner stated that he was born and
brought up village Bedlengkhaiti under Sorbhog Police Station in the district of Barpeta. He is a
permanent resident of village Tekaimari under Sorbhog Police Station. His father was Munsar
Ali Sheikh whose name was enlisted as a voter in the voters lists of 1966 and 1970 in respect of
Bijni Constituency. Petitioner’s name appeared in the voters lists of 1989 and 1994. Mother’s
name was Ahima Khatun. In the supporting affidavit, petitioner disclosed his age as 48 years.

9. Though vital material facts, such as, date or year of birth of the petitioner, names of
paternal grandparents etc. were not disclosed by the petitioner but from whatever were
disclosed by the petitioner what is discernible is that according to the petitioner his father was
Munsar Ali Sheikh who was a citizen of India. Therefore, being his son, he was a citizen of
India.
Page No.# 4/6

10. Let us now examine whether petitioner could prove the above
facts in issue.

11. In his evidence-in-chief filed by way of affidavit, petitioner stated more or less the
same thing as in the written statement. The evidence-in-chief was filed on 29.04.2016 and the
petitioner disclosed his age as 48 years. This would mean that petitioner was born sometime in
the year 1968.

12. On a query by the Tribunal, petitioner stated that father and mother had expired in
1970 and before 1980 respectively. He stated that his name was wrongly mentioned as Halim
Sheikh instead of Halim Uddin in the voters list of 1994.

13. One Juron Ali filed evidence-in-chief by way of affidavit as DW 2 stating that
petitioner Hanif Uddin was his elder brother. On a query by the Court, he stated that names of
his parents were enlisted in the voters lists of 1966 and 1970.

14. Proceeding to the documents filed by the petitioner, we find that Ext. A is a
photostat copy of voters list extract for the year 1966 in respect of Bijni Constituency. Here the
sole voter was Munsar Ali Sheikh, son of Hasen Uddin Sheikh. Ext- B is photostat copy of the
voters list of 1970 in respect of Bijni Constituency where the two voters were Munsar Ali
Sheikh, son of Hasen and Ahima Khatun, wife of Munsar. They were shown as residents of
village Bedlengkhaiti under Bijni Police Station. On a comparison of Exts. A & B, we find that
Ahima Khatun was conspicuous by her absence in the voters list of 1966 though according to
the deposition of Juron Ali (DW 2) both were voters in 1966 and 1970.

15. Ext. C is a photostat copy of voters list extract of 1989 in respect of Sorbhog
Constituency. Here the three voters were Rahima Khatun, wife of Munsar Ali; Joynal Ali, son
of Munsar; and Hanifuddin, son of Munsar. They were shown as residents of village Tekaimari
under Sorbhog Police Station. Interestingly, there is no mention about DW 2, Juron Ali, in Ext-
C.

16. In Exts. A & B, Munsar Ali Sheikh and Ahima Khatun were residents of village
Bedlengkhaiti under Bijni Police Station of Bijni Constituency whereas Hanifuddin and others of
Page No.# 5/6
Ext-C were residents of village Tekaimari under Sorbhog Police Station of Sorbhog
Constituency. While in Ext-B (1970) it was Ahima Khatun, wife of Munsar but in Ext-C (1989) it
was Rahima Khatun, wife of Munsar Ali. Therefore, it is quite evident that the voters of Ext-C
had no nexus with the two voters of Ext-B, names and places of residence being different.

17. In Ext-D, which is photostat copy of voters list of 1994 in respect of Sorbhog
Constituency, Hanifuddin was conspicuous by his absence. The three names which appeared in
the 1994 voters list (Ext-D) were Rahima Khatun, wife of Munsar, aged 45 years; Halim Sheikh,
son of Munsar, aged 25 years; and Joynal Hoque, son of Munsar, aged 22 years. According to
the petitioner, in 1994 his name was wrongly mentioned as Halim Sheikh instead of Hanif
Uddin. We are afraid we can accept such contention inasmuch as Joynal Ali of Ext-C
disappeared thereafter and in 1994 (Ext-D) the name was Joynal Hoque but with decreased
age.

18. Ext. E is a photostat copy of jamabandi copy where one of the pattadars was Alima
Khatun. There is no presence of the petitioner here. According to the petitioner, his mother
had expired before 1980. If that be so she could not have appeared in Exts. C (1989) and D
(1994).

19. Ext. F is a certificate dated 27.12.2015 issued by the Gaonburah of Tekaimari village
certifying that Md. Hanifuddin was the son of Lt. Munsar Ali Sheikh. According to the
petitioner, he was born and brought up at village Bedlengkhaiti under Sorbhog Police Station in
the district of Barpeta. Therefore, Gaonburah of Tekaimari village perhaps could not have
issued the said certificate. Moreover, parents had expired in 1970 and before 1980 respectively.
If that be so, then it is not known as to when petitioner migrated from Bedlangkhaiti village to
Tekaimari village. On what basis the Gaonburah issued the certificate has not been disclosed.
That apart, the Gaonburah did not depose before the Tribunal alongwith the
contemporaneous record to prove Ext. F and the contents thereof. Therefore, Ext. F cannot be
said to be a valid piece of evidence.

20. Ext. G is a photostat copy of the voters list of 1997 in respect of Sorbhog
Constituency. Here the two voters were Joynal Abedin, son of Munsar and Juran Ali, son of
Page No.# 6/6
Munsar. But what happened to Hanif Ali @ Hanif Uddin? Why his name did not appear in the
voters list of 1997? These are legitimate questions but there are no answers.

21. The last of the exhibits is an Elector Photo Identity Card in the name of Juran Ali
whose relations name was mentioned as Munsar. This is not a document in the name of the
petitioner and therefore it has no relevance in so far the
fact in issue is concerned.

22. Sum total of the above discussion is that petitioner failed to establish his linkage
with Munsar Ali Sheikh who he claimed to be his father and a citizen of India. Therefore, it is
evident that petitioner had failed to discharge his burden under Section 9 of the
Foreigners Act,
1946 to prove that he was not a foreigner but a citizen of India.
23. Resultantly, we do not find any error or infirmity in the view taken by the Tribunal.
24. Writ petition is dismissed. Interim order passed earlier stands vacated.

25. Registry to send down the LCR forthwith and inform the concerned Foreigners’
Tribunal, Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police (B) for taking follow-up steps.

26. Copies of this order may also be furnished to learned Standing Counsel, Election
Commission of India and State Coordinator, NRC, Assam.

The petitioner says that he is in possession of 10 Ares of
land, comprised of in Sy.No.48/3 (Re.Sy.No.48/80) of the
Kuttiadi Village, Vadakara; and that he is aggrieved by the
alignment now proposed by the third respondent, for the
purpose of construction of the “Kuttiadi Bypass” starting
from Kuttiadi – Perambra Road.

2. According to the petitioner, he had requested the
third respondent to consider an alternative alignment, so that
his property and an ongoing commercial construction thereon
could have been saved without disturbing anybody else; and
he alleges that in spite of the fact that he had the said
request validly, it has not been yet considered by the
competent Authority.

3. The petitioner says that, therefore, he approached
this Court earlier by filing W.P.(C) No.14026 of 2019, which
culminated in Ext.P4 judgment, whereby, he was directed to
be given an opportunity of being heard; but alleges that, in
WP(C) NO. 3919 OF 2021
4
spite of the specific directions in Ext.P4, none of the
materials relied upon by the competent Authority had been
given to him when the hearing was conducted, and therefore,
that this exercise was reduced to a mere eyewash. He thus
prays that the alignment now proposed by the respondents be
directed to be redone in a manner so as to avoid his property.

4. The afore submissions of Sri.P.G.Jayashankar, the
learned counsel for the petitioner, were vehemently refuted
by Sri.K.V.Manoj Kumar, the learned standing counsel for
the third respondent. He submitted that a statement has been
filed, wherein, Annexure R3(1) sketch of the alignment has
been produced and argued that the allegation of the
petitioner, that his request had not been considered at all, is
wholly untrue because it was, in fact, assessed carefully and
the original alignment was, consequently, shifted 2.6 meters
towards North, so as to substantially save his property. The
learned standing counsel then added that the original request
of the petitioner was to shift the alignment 4 meters towards
North, but that this could not be acceded to because this
would entail demolition of other residential buildings, as also
WP(C) NO. 3919 OF 2021
5
the change of the entire alignment of the road. He submitted
that, in such circumstances, the petitioner cannot have any
case against Annexure R3(1), particularly because it has been
settled with the assistance of the competent experts and
foremost agencies who are engaged in the construction of
roads and other infrastructural facilities.

5. In reply, Sri.P.G.Jayashankar conceded that Annexure
R3(1) has modified the alignment to some extent, but prayed
that, since his client's request for changing it to 4 meters
towards North has not been fully acceded to, the reliefs
sought for in this writ petition be granted.

6. Sri.M.C.John, learned counsel appearing for
respondents 6 and 7, submitted that the prayer of the
petitioner in this writ petition is extremely malicious because
he wants to solely save his his property, but at the cost of his
client's. He submitted that this has been clearly stated so in
Ext.P7 and therefore, prayed that this writ petition be
dismissed.

7. When I evaluate the afore rival contentions very
carefully, I am afraid that I cannot find favour with the
WP(C) NO. 3919 OF 2021
6
petitioner's request. This is because, it has been well settled
by this Court and by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, through a
series of judgments, that in matters which involve expert
opinion and policy decision making, this Court substitute its
wisdom for that of the experts or the competent Authorities.
Since Annexure R3(1) has been issued taking note of the
petitioner's request and acceding to it partially, I cannot find
merit in the further grievance impelled by the petitioner,
particularly when he does not contest that if the alignment is
shifted as requested by him, it would cause detriment to
various other persons and their properties. It is needless to
say that the petitioner's property cannot be saved by causing
detriment to other similarly situated persons.
In the afore circumstances, I dismiss this writ petition
without acceding to the prayers of the petitioner.
At this time, Sri.P.G.Jayashankar, the learned counsel
for the petitioner submitted that this Court may leave liberty
to his client to invoke all his other remedies, including for the
purpose of valuation of his property.

It goes without saying that the petitioner is entitled to
all eligible remedies, which are statutorily sanctioned and it
does not require any specific order from this Court for him to
invoke the same.

that the entitlement of the petitioner for appointment on

If admittedly the candidates, who are lower in merit, have
been granted appointment, those who are above them in
the merit cannot be denied such right of appointment.
Seniority as per the rules in the case of direct recruitment

1. Apprehending arrest in connection with Crime No.58/2016
registered at Police Station- Pendra, District – Bilaspur (C.G.), for
offence punishable under Section 420, 467, 468, 471, 170, 34 of
Indian Penal Code, the applicant has preferred this second bail
application U/s. 438 of Cr.P.C. for grant of anticipatory bail. The first
bail application was dismissed on 01.04.2016 in M.Cr.C.(A)
No.300/2016.

2. Case of the prosecution in brief is that, in the year 2009 the
applicant along-with other co-accused came to the complainant
personifying themselves as employees of BSNL and offered him
that in case he allows a tower to be installed in his land, an amount
of Rs.1,50,000/- would be paid and further rent of Rs.5000/- per
month would also be paid. Subsequent to that, on one day, the
applicant came to the complainant and gave him two cheques of
Rs.7000/- and Rs.5000/- and after gaining the confidence, it was
stated that in order to install the tower asked the complainant to pay
Rs.75,000/- and on such assurance Rs.75,000/- was paid to
Madhukar Dwivedi, the other accused. Subsequently when the
tower was not installed the complainant inquired and went to the
house of Madhukar Dwivedi where this applicant who was stated to
be the SDO Telephones was also present and ultimately the
amount was not returned. When the enquiry was made at BSNL
Office, Bilaspur, the personification of the applicant was found to be
forged.

3. Learned counsel for the applicant would submit that bail of another
accused namely Madhukar Dwivedi, son of the present applicant
was considered in M.Cr.C. No.7294/2016 on 13.12.2016 and the
bail was granted to Madhukar Dwivedi on the ground that entire
amount has been paid back and there has been some monetary
transaction existing between the parties. Therefore, the counsel
prays that the applicant may be extended the benefit of anticipatory
bail.

4. Per contra, learned counsel for the State opposes the bail
application, however, he do not dispute the fact that amount alleged
has already been returned.
5. I have heard the learned counsel for the parties.

6. Perused the earlier order dated 13.12.2016 in M.Cr.C.
No.7294/2016, wherein Madhukar Dwivedi has been enlarged on
bail specially taking into the fact that entire amount has been
returned. In view of this, the amount appears to have been
returned. Considering the same and the facts and circumstances of
the case, this Court is inclined to extend the benefit of anticipatory
bail to the applicant as the custodial interrogation of the applicant
may not be required in this case.

7. Accordingly, the anticipatory bail application is allowed and it is
directed that in the event of arrest of the applicant in connection
with the aforesaid offence, he shall be released on bail by the
officer arresting him on executing a personal bond in sum of
Rs.25,000/- with one surety in the like sum to the satisfaction of the
concerned Investigating Officer. The applicant shall also abide by
the following conditions :
(i) that the applicant shall make himself available for
interrogation before the investigating officer as and when required;
(ii) that the applicant shall not, directly or indirectly, make any
inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the
facts of the case so as to dissuade him/her from disclosing such
facts to the Court or to any police officer;
(iii) that the applicant shall not act, in any manner, which will be
prejudicial to fair and expeditious trial; and
(iv) that the applicant shall appear before the trial Court on each
and every date given to him by the said Court till disposal of the
trial.

APPLICATION FOR ANTICIPATORY BAIL
The applicants apprehend arrest in Crime No.1095 of 2020
of Angamali Police Station, Ernakulam, for having allegedly committed
offences punishable under Sections 304 and read with Section 34 of
the IPC and subsequently, Section 135 of the Electricity Act has also
been incorporated. The 1st applicant is the father of the 2nd applicant.
The crime was originally registered under Section 174 of the Cr.P.C,
for the death of one Sonet, which took place on 01.08.2020 at about
22.45 hours and resulted in grievous injury to one Robin.

2. The prosecution case, in brief, is that the 1st applicant had
taken on lease, certain land for tapioca cultivation. With intention to
protect his tapioca cultivation from vermin like boar etc, he installed
wires with electricity passing through it in a negligent manner, that
the deceased and his friend Robin tripped on that and got
electrocuted. As a result of which, the deceased succumbed to the
B.A.No.5030 OF 2020
3
injuries, while his friend was injured.

3. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the applicants and
the learned Public Prosecutor. The learned Public Prosecutor submits
that the 2nd applicant has not yet been arraigned as an accused and
therefore, the apprehension of his arrest is misplaced. However, he
admits that the 1st accused has been arrayed as an accused. Hence,
the present application for anticipatory bail is concerning only the 1st
applicant.

4. The learned Public Prosecutor vehemently opposed the
application for bail on the ground that it was a wanton act of the 1st
applicant, with the knowledge that it would cause death of some
person, since the electricity was drawn from the main line using wires,
anyone who came into contact would have got killed. And therefore,
there was intention to kill persons who attempted to trespass. Hence,
an offence under Section 304 of the IPC is squarely attracted to this
case, submits the learned prosecutor. The applicant will have to be
interrogated. The wires, etc., used for charging the fence will have to
be recovered and the role of the 2nd applicant will also have to be
investigated into. There is a possibility that he also may be implicated
B.A.No.5030 OF 2020
4
as an accused. Under the circumstances, it is submitted that
anticipatory bail may not be granted to the 1st applicant.

5. The learned counsel appearing for the applicants submit
that electricity was passed through the fence only with the help of a
generator and the deceased and his friends had come there for fishing
in the brook nearby. They were also using a generator. Somehow,
their generator got spoiled and they attempted to use the generator,
which was placed by the applicants. That resulted in the accidental
death. The applicant had no intention to cause the death to anyone,
nor did he have the knowledge that his act would cause death. Hence,
offence under Section 304 of the IPC is not attracted. He is entitled
to a pre arrest bail. It is stated that he is a clergyman, not involved in
any criminal case. Considering the present pandemic situation, he may
be released on bail. He is willing to co-operate with the investigation.

6. Having considered the entire facts and circumstances of
this case, anxiously, I find that the application is to be dismissed as
far as the 2nd applicant is concerned, because he is not yet implicated
as an accused. And, therefore, his apprehension of arrest is
misplaced. As far as the 1st applicant is concerned, he had allegedly
B.A.No.5030 OF 2020
5
used wires for passing electricity through his fence, which caused the
death of a person and injury to another. I find no reasons for his
absconding. He does not have any antecedents. Considering the
present pandemic situation, he need not be incarcerated. He is willing
to co-operate with the investigation. And, hence, the application of
seeking anticipatory bail as far as the 1st applicant is concerned is to
be allowed.

7. In the result, the application is allowed in part and the 1st
applicant is directed to surrender before the Investigating Officer
within two weeks. After interrogation and recovery if any, he shall be
released on bail on execution of bond for Rs.50,000/-(Rupees Fifty
thousand only), with two solvent sureties, each for the like amount to
the satisfaction of the Investigating Officer and on following further
conditions:
(i) He shall appear before the Investigating Officer as and
when called for.
(ii) He shall not intimidate or influence witnesses or tamper
with evidence.
(iii) He shall not get involved in similar offences during the
B.A.No.5030 OF 2020
6
currency of the bail period.
In case of breach of any of the bail conditions, the
prosecution shall be at liberty to apply for cancellation of the bail.
The bail application is allowed in part.

S. N. Prasad, J. This writ petition has been filed for the following reliefs:
“(i) direct/order the opp.parties to consider the case of the petitioner for
appointment/engagement under the opposite parties company as pr the
Rehabilitation Assistance Scheme formulated by the opposite parties company
as a land oustee member;
(ii) pass such other order(s) or issue direction(s) as may be deemed
fit and proper in the bonafide interest of justice.xx”

2. The factual aspect of the case is that landed property of the
petitioner‟s family was about Ac.0.49 decimal under Khata No.1073, plot
No.4365 of mouza-Kangula recorded in the name of Braja Mohan Rath, has
been acquired for NALCO vide L.A.Case No.1/89 for I.A.P.L. Notice under
2
section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act,1894 was issued by the Industries
Department of the Government of Orissa vide letter no.10944 dated
24.4.1991 to provide rehabilitation assistance to one person from each family
whose land has been acquired, husband of the petitioner was the nominee by
the family members/awardee for employment under the Scheme, but due to
non-possession of minimum matric qualification he is disqualified for job
under the said scheme, at that point of time as per the scheme whereas other
similarly situated persons who had passed the minimum qualification, they
were engaged.
It is further case of the petitioner that at the time of acquisition of
land, opposite parties have agreed to provide a job to one of the family
members but the same has not been followed and as such the writ petition was
filed being O.J.C.No.10706 of 1999 and the matter was disposed of on
16.8.2010, in the said writ petition the scheme was challenged but the writ
petition was dismissed with direction that if the petitioner has not received
financial assistance offered in lieu of employment, the same may be
considered. Accordingly, the authorities are taking steps to give financial
assistance but the petitioner‟s family refused to accept the same, in the light of
this order this writ petition has been filed.

3. Counter affidavit has been filed on behalf of the opposite parties
wherein, inter alia, it has been stated that the petitioner is not coming under
the purview of consideration for appointment being not coming under the
definition of „family‟ rather she is coming under the definition of „nominee‟ as
per the definition made in the scheme and the scheme contains a condition
that the offer of appointment would only be given to the family which contains
the definition the awardee, his/her spouse and dependent unmarried
son/daughter. Since petitioner is the nominee of Chaturbhuj Rath, daughter-
in-law of the original awardee and as such she cannot be given benefit of
appointment.
It has been submitted that the opposite parties are taking all
efforts to extend benefit of financial assistance as has been directed by this
3
Court in O.J.C.No.10706 of 1999 and other analogous cases, she is not
accepting it. It has been submitted that appointment under the
Rehabilitation Assistance Scheme can only be given to such person who is
entitled to get as per the scheme.

4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
documents available on record.

5. Undisputed fact in this case is that land of father of one
Chaturbhuj Rath was acquired on 24.4.1991 since on that date notification
under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act,1894 was issued. Husband of
the petitioner, who was son of the original awardee, was minor during the
relevant time and as such he has not been given benefit of engagement being
not eligible as per the qualification prescribed under the Scheme, hence the
writ petition had been filed challenging the eligibility condition before this
Court being O.J.C.No.10706 of 1999. Husband of the petitioner was one of the
petitioners being petitioner no.6 and the said writ petition was disposed of with
the observation that that petitioner in those writ petition may be considered for
financial benefit in lieu of employment. After disposal of the said writ petition
on 16.8.2010, this writ petition has been filed on 4.9.2012 by the wife of
Chaturbhuj Rath, petitioner no.6 in O.J.C. No.10706 of 1999, praying to
provide her beneit of appointment under the scheme.

6. We have examined the scheme as well as the definition of „family‟
which includes awardee, his/her spouse and dependent unmarried
son/daughter. Nominee has been defined as the member of the family
nominated by the awardee for the purpose of receiving benefits under this
scheme. Awardee has been defined as a person to whom compensation was
awarded for the land acquired for IAPL. Petitioner herein is the wife of
Chaturbhuj Rath and daughter-in-law of Chaturbhuj Rath, hence being
daughter-in-law of the original awardee, she will not come under the definition
of „family‟. The scheme provides that offer of appointment can only be given to
the member of the family i.e. awardee, his/her spouse and dependent
unmarried son/daughter and not daughter-in-law.
4
It is settled that offer of appointment can be given under the
scheme and for that purpose the scheme has been prepared in the shape
of Rehabilitation Assistance Scheme. It is further settled that offer of
appointment can only be given as per the provision of the scheme otherwise
not. We have found that the petitioner is the daughter-in-law of the original
awardee who is not coming under the definition of „family‟, hence she cannot
be said to be entitled to get appointment under the scheme.
Taking into consideration the facts stated herein above, we find
that the petitioner has failed to make out a case and accordingly, we decline to
interfere with the same.

7. In the result, the writ petition is dismissed being devoid of merit.

34 OF IPC AND SECTION 3(1)(x) OF SC/ST (POA) ACT.
THIS CRIMINAL PETITION COMING ON FOR ADMISSION
THIS DAY, THE COURT MADE THE FOLLOWING.
ORDER
1. A private complaint in PCR No.09/2017 came to be filed
before the Civil Judge, JMFC, Mandya under Section 200
of Cr.P.C. on 10.05.2017 alleging that on 02.08.2015,
when the complainant after getting down from the KSRTC
bus stand, Mandya at about 5.00 p.m. was about to
board a bus to go to Mysuru, at that time, accused Nos.4
to 8 being employees of Best Life Foundation, Mysuru,
abducted the complainant forcefully in a van and took
him to Best Life Foundation and confined him there from
02.08.2015 to 02.01.2016 for the sake of money.
- 3 -
CRL.P No. 967 of 2020
2. It is alleged that the complainant was ill-treated during
the course of his confinement. In that background, a
private complaint came to be filed alleging offences under
Sections 323, 504, 357, 362, 367, 368 of IPC and Section
3(i) (x) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes
(Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

3. The learned Magistrate having taken cognizance referred
the matter to Mandya West Police Station for enquiry
under Section 156(3) of Cr.P.C. for investigation.
Thereafter, investigation was carried out and charge
sheet has been laid. The petitioner is before this Court
being aggrieved by the same seeking for the aforesaid
relief.

4. Sri.Sunil Kumar.H, learned counsel appearing for the
petitioner would submit that a private complaint which
has been filed is not in compliance with the dicta laid
down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in PRIYANKA
SRIVASTA AND ANOTHER v. STATE OF UTTAR
PRADESH AND OTHERS - (2015)6 SCC 287, more
- 4 -
CRL.P No. 967 of 2020
particularly in para No.21 thereof which is reproduced
hereunder for easy reference:-
21. Dealing with the nature of power
exercised by the Magistrate under Section
156(3) CrPC, a three-Judge Bench in
Devarapalli Lakshminarayana Reddy v. V.
Narayana Reddy, had to express thus:
(SCC p.258, para 17)
"17. ... It may be noted
further that an order made under
sub-section (3) of Section 156, is in
the nature of a peremptory
reminder or intimation to the police
to exercise their plenary powers of
investigation under Section 156(1).
Such an investigation embraces the
entire continuous process which
beings with the collection of
evidence under Section 156 and
ends with a report or charge-sheet
under Section 173."

5. He submits that there is no averment made in the private
complaint as regards complainant having approached the
jurisdictional police for lodging a complainant, refusal by
the said Station House Officer, the approach made by the
complainant to the Superior Officer and no action being
taken by such Superior Officer apart therefrom, he
submits that there is no verifying affidavit verifying the
contents of the said complainant as such, the Magistrate
- 5 -
CRL.P No. 967 of 2020
ought to have taken these factors into account and not
referred the matter for investigation without such
compliance. He submits that complainant has been
hospitalized for treatment for deaddiction of his alcohol
addiction and various Psychiatric disorder as regards
which he has treated during the said period. In support
thereof various medical certificates, prescriptions and
clinical examination are also produced along with the
petition. Therefore, he submits that even on merits, the
complainant being a patient who has been treated at the
hospital and discharged on 02.01.2016 has filed a
complaint on 10.05.2017 which is after a period nearly 14
months from his discharge, which establishes malafides
on the part of the complainant and on this ground also he
submits that the petition is required to be allowed and
the criminal proceedings needs to be quashed.

6. One Sri.Nagaraju, learned counsel who has entered
appearance for respondent No.2 - complainant in the
other matter, on enquiry whether he would be appearing
in this matter and address argument, he submits that he
has no instruction.
- 6 -
CRL.P No. 967 of 2020

7. Learned HCGP for the respondent No.1 would submit that
a charge sheet has been filed. Hence, reference to the
judgment of Priyanka Srivastava's case would not
arise. This Court ought to dismiss the petition and the
matter proceed for trial.

8. Heard Sri.Sunil Kumar.H, learned counsel for the
petitioner. Sri.Mahesh Shetty, learned HCGP for
respondent No.1. Perused the papers.

9. A perusal of the complaint would indicate that there is no
particular averment which would been made as regards
the complainant having approached the jurisdictional
Station House Officer, his refusal to register a complaint,
the petitioner approaching the Higher Officers and their
refusal to file a complaint before filing of the private
complaint, thus, it is clear that the said complaint fails on
the dicta laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court in
Priyanka Srivastava's case supra.

10. As regards the contention of learned HCGP that since the
charge sheet has been laid, the question of dicta laid
- 7 -
CRL.P No. 967 of 2020
down by the Priyanka Srivastava's case would not arise.
This Court in Crl.P.No.907/2018 between Manjula.M v.
State of Karnataka by its order dated 08.04.2022, has
come to a conclusion that once there is a violation of the
dicta laid down in Priyanka Srivastava's filing of a
charge sheet would not be any consequence. Hence, the
submission made by Sri.Mahesh Shetty, learned HCGP
would not survive for consideration.

11. Having perused the complaint there being a violation of
the principles laid down by the Apex Court in Priyanka
Srivastava's case, I am of the considered opinion,
criminal proceedings cannot continue, as such, I pass the
following:-
ORDER
i. The petition is allowed.
ii. The FIR and complaint registered in
Spl.C.37/2018 pending on the file of I
Additional District and Sessions Judge,
Mandya, is hereby quashed.
Consequently, the charge sheet which has
been laid down in the said proceedings is
also quashed.
- 8 -
CRL.P No. 967 of 2020
iii. Liberty is however reserved to the petitioner
to comply with the requirements of the
Priyanka Srivastava's case and initiate
fresh proceedings if so desires.

1. The appellant, who was original accused
Page 1 of 13
R/CR.A/3192/2008 JUDGMENT
in Sessions Case No. 83 of 2007, is before us by
way of this appeal, whereby, he has challenged
the judgment and order of the learned Additional
Sessions Judge and Presiding Officer, Fast Track
Court, Dahod, Dated : 11.06.2008, whereby, he was
convicted for the offence punishable under
Section 302 of the IPC and was sentenced to
undergo imprisonment for life and to pay fine of
Rs.1000/- and in default to undergo further
rigorous imprisonment for three months.

2. The brief facts of the case of the
prosecution reads as under;

3. A declaration was made by the appellant,
herein, before Jhalod Police Station on
31.05.2007, wherein, he stated that, on
30.12.2007, after taking supper he along with his
elder son and his mother went to sleep outside
the house, whereas, his wife, namely Sharda -
the deceased, was sleeping inside the house along
with their minor son and the door was locked from
inside. It is, further, stated by the appellant,
therein, that at about 03:00 a.m. his son started
crying, and therefore, he knocked the door of his
house, but, the deceased did not respond. The
appellant, therefore, entered into his house
through roof and in the light of fire, he found
that the deceased had committed suicide by
Page 2 of 13
R/CR.A/3192/2008 JUDGMENT
hanging herself. The appellant, then, informed
his relatives and on their arrival, police was
came to be intimated and the same was registered
vide Accidental Death Entry No. 7 of 2007 and the
investigation was commenced. After the recording
of Inquest Panchnama and other procedure, a
complaint was given by the father of the
deceased, wherein, it was alleged that the
appellant used to consume liquor and keep doubt
about the character of the deceased and he also
used to beat and harass her, on account of which
the deceased frequently used to come to her
parental home. It was, further, stated in the
complaint given by the father of the deceased
that just a few months before the alleged
offence, a writing was given by the appellant in
the presence of panchas that he would not keep
doubt about the character of the deceased and
would not maltreat her. Moreover, before about 15
days prior to the alleged incident, the deceased
had come to her parental house and had informed
them that the appellant was threatening her of
dire consequences. The father of the deceased,
then, stated that on 31.05.2007, he was informed
that the deceased had committed suicide by
hanging herself. The father of the deceased
further stated that, since, the deceased was
complaining of threats issued by the appellant of
dire consequences, he was filing the complaint
Page 3 of 13
R/CR.A/3192/2008 JUDGMENT
against the appellant for necessary legal
actions. The complaint given by the father of the
deceased came to be registered vide I- C. R. No.
76 of 2007. On registration of the offence,
police carried out the investigation and since,
prima facie, case was made out against the
appellant, charge-sheet was filed against him.

4. To bring home the charges leveled
against the appellant, the prosecution examined
the following witnesses;
